reads.purpose: SKILL.md frontmatter: "Remove AI writing patterns from prose. Use when drafting, editing, or reviewing text to eliminate predictable AI tells." README: "AI writing has patterns. Predictable phrases, structures, rhythms. This skill teaches Claude (or any LLM) to catch and remove them." It is a short style checklist aimed at blog/essay prose (it refers to "the essay" and "another post"), with phrase lists, structure tables, a pre-delivery quick-check list and a 5-dimension self-score. It does NOT target AI-detector bypass. Searching every .md file for detect, bypass, watermark, GPTZero, Turnitin, perplex, burst, typo, unicode and invisible found nothing, and no rule mentions detectors. The closest thing is the self-score dimension "Authenticity | Sounds human?". It is also not a watermark remover. Missing entirely: any no-fabrication or meaning-preservation guardrail, any carve-outs (quotations, academic or technical register, methods-section passive, required conclusions), any handling of the user's own voice, and any genre modes. The rules are absolute ("Kill all adverbs", "No passive constructions", "No em dashes at all", "Three-item lists | Use two items or one").

invents_facts.what: Before: "In today's fast-paced landscape, we need to lean into discomfort and navigate uncertainty with clarity. This matters because your competition isn't waiting." After: "Move faster. Your competition is." The output adds a new imperative about speed (the input only called the landscape "fast-paced") and a new claim that competitors are moving faster. It drops discomfort, uncertainty and clarity. The result is an invented slogan, and it ends on the punchy one-liner the skill itself bans.

Before: "It turns out that most teams struggle with alignment. The uncomfortable truth is that nobody wants to admit they're confused." After: "Teams struggle with alignment. Nobody admits confusion." Deleting "most" (labelled "Cut hedging") makes a qualified claim universal. "nobody wants to admit" (a reluctance) becomes "Nobody admits" (an absolute behavioral claim). The output also uses the lazy extreme "Nobody" that the skill bans.

Before: "Not because the technology is complex. Because people are complex." After: "Technology is manageable. People aren't." The output adds an evaluative claim the input never made (technology is "manageable"). It also turns "people are complex" into "people are not manageable".

Model fix: "The team fixed it that week" beats "the complaint becomes a fix." The after-text adds an actor ("the team") and a time frame ("that week") that the input phrase did not contain. That teaches the model to invent specifics when it de-personifies a sentence.

invents_facts.where: references/structures.md Passive Voice table, lines 99-106; SKILL.md rule 3
invents_facts.what: Instructions: "X was created" -> "Name who created it", "It is believed that" -> "Name who believes it", "Mistakes were made" -> "Name who made them", "The decision was reached" -> "Name who decided", plus "Every sentence needs a human subject". Nothing limits the named actor to one stated in the source. When the input withholds the actor, the model must supply one, for example an invented belief-holder or decision-maker.

invents_facts.where: SKILL.md rule 4 and quick check (lines 21, 44); references/phrases.md line 128
invents_facts.what: "Vague declarative (\"The implications are significant\")? Name the specific implication." and "cut it or replace it with the specific thing." These invite the model to write implications or reasons the input did not state. Cutting is offered only as an alternative, and no source constraint exists.
"'What makes this hard is...' becomes 'The constraint is...' or better, name the specific constraint." The preferred ("better") path adds a specific constraint that may not be in the input.

"You don't sit down one day and decide to..." beats "Nobody designed this." The rewrite turns a one-line observation into an imagined second-person scene (sitting down one day, deciding) that the input did not contain. "Put the reader in the room" and "Specifics beat abstractions" generalize the move.
Lazy extremes -> "Use specifics instead of sweeping claims." Replacing "every/always/never" with specifics, with no instruction to use only source facts, invites invented counts or examples.

The "Problem" column rewrites carry new content: "a bet lives or dies in days" -> "Someone kills the project or ships it"; "the market rewards" -> "Buyers pay for things"; "the data tells us" -> "Someone reads it and draws a conclusion". These reinterpretations add actors and outcomes (a project, shipping, buyers) that the input phrases never named.

detector_tricks: No explicit detector-bypass tricks. There are no typos, homoglyphs, invisible or zero-width characters, deliberate errors, synonym spinning or perplexity tricks. A search of all .md files for detect, bypass, watermark, GPTZero, Turnitin, perplex, burst, typo, unicode and invisible found nothing. The only non-ASCII characters in the installed files are the em dash in examples.md:45 and the box-drawing characters in the README file tree.

Burstiness-like rules framed as style, not evasion: "Mix sentence lengths", "Three consecutive sentences match length? Break one." (a mechanical length-variance check), and the absolute "No em dashes at all" ban. These overlap with detector-gaming advice, but the repo never connects them to detectors.
The self-score dimension "Authenticity | Sounds human?" is judged by the model itself, not by a detector.
self_evidence: None. README.md and CHANGELOG.md report no test, benchmark, human or LLM judging, detector result, sample size or evaluator. The only quality mechanism is the model's own 1-10 self-score on 5 dimensions with a "Below 35/50: revise" threshold, and that is an instruction, not a reported result.
No evals, test corpus or scripts ship in the repo. The installed files are SKILL.md and references/{phrases,structures,examples}.md, plus README.md, CHANGELOG.md and LICENSE.

Context, not maintainer evidence: our 2026-10-20 survey cites issue #229 on blader/humanizer, which found that rule-driven rewrites create a new clipped, uniform-beat tell. That measurement was of a different repo and must not be attributed to stop-slop.

reads.purpose: SKILL.md frontmatter: "Rewrite AI-sounding text so it reads like the writer without changing what it says. Use when editing or reviewing prose for AI tells: not-X-but-Y contrasts, one-line closers, staged openers, forced triads, dashes everywhere, inflated claims, sales language, stock AI words, bold labels, or filler." It is an editing skill built on Wikipedia's "Signs of AI writing" (WikiProject AI Cleanup) and it explains every tell as the model's 'default choice for the widest range of readers'. It does NOT target AI-detector bypass. README: "Humanizer edits for human readers. It does not try to get past AI detectors, and detectors still flag most of its output." Release 3.0.0 removed the `ai-detection` keyword from the package files. Agent manifests describe it the same way (openai.yaml default prompt: "rewrite this text in my voice without changing its facts"). The README is now headed "sponsored by cfo.ai".

Step 3 only checks that facts were not dropped or changed, so added facts are never checked. CHANGELOG 4.0.0: "The skill no longer forbids adding facts... This reverses the no-invention rule from 2.9.0. Patterns 14 and 17 follow the same change."
For blog posts, essays and personal writing: "you may add a reaction where the writer would". This adds opinions or reactions the input never contained.

The model fills in relationships and sources from its own knowledge: §14 "Name the relationship. If you do not know it, keep the vague wording." §17 "When you know the real source and what it said, name it."

Before: "...the Haolai River is of interest to researchers and conservationists. Experts believe it plays a crucial role in the regional ecosystem." After: "Researchers and conservationists study the Haolai River, often called the narrowest river in the world: it averages about 15 centimeters wide." Adds a superlative and a measurement (15 cm) that are not in the input, and drops the ecosystem claim.

Before: "Her views have been cited in The New York Times, BBC, Financial Times, and The Hindu. She maintains an active social media presence with over 500,000 followers." After: "In a 2024 New York Times interview, she argued that AI regulation should focus on outcomes rather than methods." Invents a year, an interview format, a topic and her opinion.

Before: "...a distinctive feature of Somali cuisine is the incorporation of camel meat... widespread adoption of pasta in the local culinary landscape..." After: "Somali cuisine also includes camel meat, which is considered a delicacy. Pasta dishes, introduced during Italian colonization, remain common, especially in the south." Adds 'considered a delicacy' and 'especially in the south'.

Before: "Let's dive into how caching works in Next.js. Here's what you need to know." After: "Next.js caches data at multiple layers, including request memoization, the data cache, and the router cache." The entire technical content is new.

Before: "Sharing one build folder nearly works. This post is about the part that doesn't. The slow part is the dependencies." After: "Sharing one build folder saves space, but one checkout can end up running another checkout's code. Most of the build time goes to the dependencies." Adds 'saves space', a specific failure mode, and 'most of the build time'.

Before: "This function was added to replace the previous approach of iterating through all items, which caused O(n²) performance." After: "This function uses a hash map for O(1) lookups, avoiding the O(n²) cost..." The hash map implementation and the O(1) complexity are not in the input.

Before: "The figures below are drawn from each vendor's published pricing; anything we could not confirm is flagged rather than guessed." After: "Prices are each vendor's published rate. Two vendors publish nothing; call them." Adds a count ('Two vendors') and an instruction ('call them').

Before: "The temple's color palette of blue, green, and gold resonates with the region's natural beauty, symbolizing Texas bluebonnets, the Gulf of Mexico..." After: "The temple is painted blue, green, and gold to evoke Texas bluebonnets and the Gulf of Mexico." Adds 'painted' and asserts design intent ('to evoke'), even though the pattern's own rule says to keep only what the source supports.

Before: "Symmetry is the language of trust. Efficiency becomes a trap when teams forget the human layer." After: "Symmetric layouts often feel more predictable to users. Teams can over-optimize workflows and miss how people use them." Interprets the aphorisms into specific claims (layouts, users, predictability). Also 'organizational readiness' becomes "whether the organization is ready to change its habits" (adds 'change its habits').

Before: "Then AlphaEvolve arrived. It had no preference for symmetry. No aesthetic prior. No nostalgia for human taste. The old rules were gone." After: "AlphaEvolve had no preference for symmetry or for designs that look human-made, so the old rules stopped applying." Adds a causal link ('so') and reinterprets 'human taste' as 'designs that look human-made'. Mild.

After adds "fixing it here means checking the merge flow for every account and backfilling the rows that are already wrong". The consequence about checking every account is inferred and was not stated in the Before (the Before's 123/6 numbers are dropped on purpose). Mild.

§13: "Korattur has recurring traffic congestion and water shortages" adds 'recurring'. §6: "with time for informal networking between sessions" adds 'informal'/'between sessions' to "networking opportunities". §1: "The heavy beat makes the song sound more aggressive" adds 'heavy'. §11: "The system preserves the results automatically" supplies an actor the input never named. reads.purpose: Per the SKILL.md frontmatter: "Edit drafts into sharper, more human writing while preserving the writer's personal voice, or detect AI-slop patterns without rewriting." It has two modes. Edit (the default) makes a minimal edit and adds a "What changed" note. Detect names each pattern, quotes the line and gives a short fix. The target is reader-perceived AI style in blog posts, LinkedIn posts, emails, product updates and personal essays (README, plugin-submission.md). It does NOT target AI-detector bypass. Detect mode refuses to guess authorship ("Do not rewrite, score the draft, or guess whether AI wrote it. AI detectors guess."). It has no watermark-removal, typo-injection, perplexity or burstiness instructions. SKILL.md and eval.md are pure ASCII (checked by grep), so there are no homoglyphs or invisible characters. The author describes his own use (plugin-submission.md) as the "middle 50%" of his process: he writes the first draft and does the final line-by-line pass himself. The installed files are skills/no-ai-slop/SKILL.md (1,715 words) and eval.md (504 words). agents/openai.yaml (about 25 words) is display metadata only. The README advertises 20+ patterns. SKILL.md has 18 bold-headed patterns plus 3 word/phrase lists.

invents_facts.what: Before: "The integration improved efficiency". After: "The integration cut deploy time from 40 minutes to 4." The after invents a metric (deploy time) and two numbers that are absent from the before. Our 2026-10-20 survey already flagged this.

Before: "The tool significantly improves engineering productivity". After: "The tool cut review time from 30 minutes to 8." The before has no specific fact to protect. The after invents a metric (review time) and two numbers. Our survey did not flag this one.

Before: "The launch adds file search, highlighting the team's commitment to better workflows". After: "The launch adds file search, so users can find old drafts without leaving the editor." The after invents a user benefit and a use case (old drafts, finding them without leaving the editor) that the input does not contain.

Before: "The launch marks a pivotal moment for the company". After: "The launch is the company's first paid product." The after invents a business fact. The rule says "State the fact", but the input contained no fact.

Before: "The app serves as a centralized hub for sponsor management". After: "The app tracks sponsors, drafts, due dates, and approvals in one place." The after invents three features (drafts, due dates, approvals).

"The team shipped it Tuesday" beats "the decision emerged." The preferred sentence is different content: an actor (team), an action (shipped) and a day (Tuesday) that "the decision emerged" does not contain. It models supplying who and when rather than restructuring.

invents_facts.where: SKILL.md line 36 (portability test) and eval.md line 16
invents_facts.what: Instruction: a generic sentence should be cut "or replace[d] ... with a fact, example, mechanism, consequence, or judgment specific to this subject". eval check 8 then asks whether every generic sentence was "cut or made specific". When the draft holds no such fact, the replace path invites invented specifics or a new opinion ("judgment"). Mitigations: SKILL.md line 30 ("Don't invent claims, examples, stats, or opinions"), line 66 ("facts already in the content") and eval check 7 ("where the draft supports them").

Instruction: "If the ending needs more closure, add a plain takeaway or next action." This tells the model to write a new closing takeaway or call to action, which can add an opinion or recommendation the writer never stated.
The skill triggers when the user wants a draft "more opinionated". Read literally, this invites adding opinions, which conflicts with the body's "Don't invent ... opinions".

reads.purpose: The skill rewrites AI-sounding text "as a specific, opinionated human". It works from a 55-pattern catalog (P1-P55), offers five preset voices (casual, professional, technical, warm, blunt) and three modes (detect, rewrite, edit), and can add an optional 0-100 "AI-tell" score. Flags: --iterate, --aggressive, --purpose, --openings, --ignore-code and --ignore-quotes. The README says "It is not an AI detector, and it does not promise to pass one" and calls passing detectors "the wrong goal". However, the skill's Burstiness and Perplexity Principles are written around what "AI detectors measure". The score rubric's 61-80 band says "detectors will probably catch it". docs/science.md cites a RAID finding that structural paraphrasing cut DetectGPT accuracy from 70.3% to 4.6% as "the reason the skill rewrites rhythm rather than vocabulary". So the skill disclaims detector bypass, but its design is detector-aware. It is NOT a watermark remover. It strips chatbot citation tokens, utm_source=chatgpt.com and zero-width/homoglyph characters, and nothing in it targets model watermarks. Size: SKILL.md (5,841 words) loads every time. On-demand references add patterns.md (3,615), always-on-templates.md (465) and patterns.zh.md (450), for a total of about 10,371 words. A separate zero-dependency Node CLI (not part of the skill) computes a fixed-formula score (0.40 lexical AI-word density + 0.28 low burstiness + 0.18 low MATTR diversity + 0.14 trigram repetition). Its `compare --check-facts` checks that every number, percentage, date, version, URL and run of capitals in the before-file is still present in the after-file. It never reports added facts and misses swapped values or meaning changes.

invents_facts.what: The instruction's own example turns 'Improves performance' into 'cuts p99 latency from 900ms to 40ms', which adds numbers absent from the input. It contradicts the no-fabrication rule a few lines above.
Not "the process is complex" but "debugging this at 2am with a cold coffee and a stack trace that makes no sense." This invents a first-person anecdote and sensory detail.

Each adds content the input lacks. #1 adds an opinion: "This API design is frustrating" beats "The API has certain limitations." #4 adds a shared-experience framing: "You know that feeling when...". #7 adds a narrative opening: "So I was looking at the logs and...". #9 adds a callback: "Remember that API I called frustrating? It gets worse.". #10 adds a staged self-correction.

detector_tricks: The Burstiness Principle is explicitly detector-framed ('AI detectors measure "burstiness"... Human writing has HIGH burstiness'). It sets numeric targets: 3-8, 12-20 and 25-40 word sentences in every paragraph, never 3+ similar lengths in a row, and a rewrite check of 'sentence-length variance > 30%'. The skill's own --score formula and the CLI score both reward this.

The Perplexity Principle is explicitly detector-framed ('AI detectors also measure "perplexity"'). It says to pick 'the second or third word that comes to mind, not the first (the most statistically likely one AI would pick)', add slang or jargon and informal transitions ('Anyway,', 'Look,'), and use unexpected analogies. This is word-choice perplexity raising.

Soul-injection 'deliberate imperfection' moves are inserted, not just preserved: fragments, one-word sentences, mid-thought starts, self-corrections, tangents, broken parallelism, abrupt endings. These are burstiness and naturalness hacks. There are no deliberate typos or grammar errors; P26 actually says to hold one quality level.

P17 treats quote style as a model fingerprint ('ChatGPT uses curly quotes; Claude uses straight quotes') and adjusts typography to match the author. P13's zero-tolerance em-dash removal deletes a surface fingerprint. patterns.md itself notes these surface tells (P7, P13, P17) are the most patchable and drift-prone.

P34 and P35 strip provenance traces left by AI tools: citation tokens (citeturn0search0, oaicite, [cite: 1], grok_card, ppl-ai-file-upload, RAG attribution tags) and utm_source=chatgpt.com / referrer=grok.com URL parameters. This is the closest thing in the skill to 'watermark removal'. These are copy-paste artifacts, not statistical or cryptographic model watermarks, and the skill has nothing that targets those.

No homoglyph or invisible-character insertion. P52 does the reverse: it strips zero-width spaces, ZWJ, soft hyphens, dense NBSP and Cyrillic/Greek homoglyphs, and the example says 'the goal is good writing, not evasion.'

The score rubric still uses detector language: band 61-80 reads 'detectors will probably catch it'. The 0-20 band said 'No detector should flag it' until v0.8.3 (2026-11-17). The logo said 'Make AI Text Undetectable' until v0.3.0.

reads.purpose: The skill audits and rewrites prose to remove "AI-isms" (AI writing patterns). It works as a writing-quality editor with three modes: rewrite (the default), detect (flag only) and edit (fix a file in place). It also has optional voice profiles, audience context profiles, house-style configs, a limit of two editing passes, and a required Verification report. SKILL.md (4,904 words) requires the model to read references/patterns.md (18,973 words) in full before any pass, so about 23.9k words load. A deterministic Node detector, a quote normalizer and a preservation validator ship with it, but the skill text runs without them and reports "model-only" when they are absent. It does NOT target AI-detector bypass. It calls its flags "signals, not proof" and cites detector false positives on non-native writers. It says the em dash and curly quotes are not authorship evidence and forbids adding mistakes to imitate a person. The README turns away sponsors whose purpose is "getting past detectors". The closest it comes to watermark removal is stripping pasted chatbot citation tokens and AI-referrer utm parameters from URLs.

invents_facts.what: Several cells tell the model to add specifics without saying they must come from the source: 'thriving | growing, active (or cite a number)', 'enduring | lasting, long-running (or cite how long)', 'marking a pivotal moment | changing [X], leading to [Y]'. The [Y] slot invites a new causal consequence. Only the file's preamble ('Replacement examples supply wording, not new facts') restrains them.

'myriad | many, numerous (or give a number)', 'plethora | many, a lot of (or give a number)', 'burgeoning | growing, emerging (or cite a number)'. These are unconditioned invitations to insert a number.

invents_facts.where: references/patterns.md, Tier 3 word and phrase tables (installed)
invents_facts.what: Unconditioned 'add specifics' fixes: 'significant / significantly | Replace some with specifics: numbers, comparisons, examples'; 'effective | Say how or cite a metric'; 'world-class / state-of-the-art / best-in-class | Cite a benchmark or comparison'; 'unprecedented | Name the precedent it breaks'; 'long-term sustainability | Cite the time horizon and the constraint'; '(sustainable) reward emissions | Cite the emission schedule and the sink'; 'tokenized incentive structures | Describe the actual mechanism (vesting, gauge, bonded LP, etc.)'. If the source has none of these, obeying the cell means inventing them.

'Cut "designed for" — either it is or it isn't. Then state the property.' This turns a stated design intent into an asserted property, which raises certainty ('designed for long-term durability' becomes 'is durable').

invents_facts.where: references/patterns.md, Tier 1A 'testament to' and 'hit differently' rows (installed)
invents_facts.what: 'testament to | shows, proves, demonstrates': 'proves' can upgrade the claim's certainty. 'hit differently | feels different, affects [me/us] differently': the slot can insert a first-person speaker the input did not have.

Before: 'The line I keep coming back to: agents are teenagers'. After: 'Agents are teenagers.' The rewrite drops the marker that this is a quoted line and presents it as the writer's own assertion, which is a stance and attribution shift. The next sentence partly mitigates this ('Attribute the comparison only when the source names its speaker').

invents_facts.what: Before: 'Imagine a world where every deploy is instant'. After: 'Every deploy would be instant.' An invitation to imagine becomes the writer's own conditional claim. This is a minor stance shift, although the rule says to keep the source's confidence.

"X may exceed Y by 2027"'; #43 'Fill in with real content or delete'; #49 'name specific things, cite specific cases'. The installed patterns.md conditions each of these on the source; the README rows do not.

invents_facts.what: 'Mix short/long, fragments, questions' tells the model to add questions and fragments that are not in the input. This contradicts the installed P94 and the never-inject 'Staccato conversion' rule.

detector_tricks: The installed SKILL.md and references/patterns.md instruct none of the classic bypass tricks: no typos, homoglyphs, zero-width or invisible characters, deliberate errors, or perplexity or burstiness padding. They forbid them outright: 'do not ... add mistakes to imitate a person' (P07); no staccato conversion (S40); vary rhythm 'not by imposing word-count bands, adding questions, or chopping sentences into fragments' (P94).

The only fingerprint or watermark-style removal is copy-paste cleanup. It strips leaked chatbot citation tokens (citeturn0search0, contentReference[oaicite:0]{index=0}, oai_citation, [attached_file:1], grok_card) and AI-referrer URL parameters (utm_source=chatgpt.com, copilot.com, openai, claude.ai, perplexity.ai, referrer=grok.com). Neither is a statistical or Unicode watermark, and no rule mentions removing invisible Unicode watermark characters or 'Claude watermarks'.

The repo's bundled detector works the other way. It flags 'bypass characters' (homoglyph letter swaps, and word joiners or zero-width characters splitting words) as evasion evidence, refined in 3.37.0/3.38.0 so that Cyrillic or Greek prose and show-notes word joiners are not misread.

Detector ignore markers (<!-- avoid-ai-writing:ignore-start --> ... <!-- avoid-ai-writing:ignore-end -->) exclude text from the repo's own detector score. They are meant for quoting AI specimens and are not part of the model-facing skill, but they would hide any text from that detector.
README pattern table row 34 (not installed) still advises 'Mix short/long, fragments, questions'. This is burstiness-style advice that the installed catalog now forbids.

These are caveats, not tricks. SKILL.md cites 'Adversarial paraphrase reduces detection accuracy by ~88% across every method tested (arXiv:2506.07001, 2025)' only as a warning that detectors are unreliable. The README says products whose purpose is 'getting past detectors aren't a fit' for sponsorship.
self_evidence: Human-control false positives (maintainer's own measurement, CHANGELOG 3.22.0, 2026-07-31). The detector's composite score fired on 0.0% of 560 human paragraphs (Wilson 95% CI 0.0–0.7%; worst paragraph 11/100). The corpus was 9 public-domain works (1788–1907) plus 25 of the maintainer's own 2019–Dec 2022 blog posts, taken from Wayback captures and checked by Jaccard similarity. It was also 0.0% on 628 paragraphs of the current versions. This measures only the detector score, not rewrite quality.

Flag-level rates on the same human text. The em-dash rule fired on 18.3% and Tier 1 words on 12.5% of the maintainer's pre-2023 paragraphs (257 paragraphs: 8.9% 1A markers, 3.5% 1B clarity edits). This is why Tier 1 was split into 1A/1B and why the 5–20x 'AI frequency' claim from brandonwise/humanizer is now labelled 'inherited, not measured'.

Machine-written corpus (CHANGELOG 3.22.0): RAID (Dugan et al. 2024, 11 model families, sampled by byte range) plus HC3 (Guo et al. 2023, paired human and ChatGPT answers). Composite ROC-AUC was 0.501 at paragraph level (HC3 0.554, RAID 0.451) and 0.623 at document level (HC3 0.654, RAID 0.599). The best operating point gave 12.8% false positives for 27.7% true positives. 'Uniformity' fired on 2.1% of human vs 25.1% of machine documents (lift 11.7x), and filler had lift 3.4x. The 112-entry vocabulary table had lift 0.9 (it fires slightly more on human text). The em dash had lift 0.2 (9.9% of human vs 1.9% of machine documents). After fixes, hedge-stack lift rose to 2.2 and em-dash false hits on human text fell from 17.9% to 13.7%. These are older model generations, and per-class sample sizes are not given in the entry.

HAP-E exploratory counts (docs/research/hape-2026-11, results dated 2026-11-03, cited in patterns.md since 3.39.0). There are 8,290 matched documents per class: human vs GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini and Llama 3 70B/8B Instruct 2024 continuations, with no Claude or newer models. Median sentence-length CV was 0.40–0.44 for the models vs 0.65 for humans. Median TTR over 200 tokens was 0.63 for humans, 0.70 for GPT-4o and 0.59–0.61 for Llama. 'Notably,'-type sentence openers ran at 2–3x the human rate in GPT-4o/4o-mini but below the human rate in Llama. Per million words: copula-swap regex 276.9/306.6 (GPT-4o/mini) and 51.2–65.4 (Llama) vs 36.2 human; hyphenated-modifier stacks 32–43 vs 53.1 human; same-opener runs of three 17.3–21.3 (GPT) and 187.4–250.2 (Llama) vs 151.5 human; stranded auxiliaries 0.3–1.1 vs 9.1 human; colon triples 19.2–27.1 vs 12.3 human. The counts are descriptive with no confidence intervals. Several catalogued 'tells' are more common in the human text.

Gate calibration, 2026-10-15 (evals/gate-calibration). On 376 human documents from 38 sources (technical context, rendered-markdown mode), 26.6% (100/376) fail at 0 allowed findings and 1.3% (5/376) at the default threshold of 6 findings per file. An earlier CHANGELOG figure (1.9% vs 31.4%) was not rerun. This does not establish authorship accuracy.

Automated rewrite regression gate for PRs #295/#296 (evals/rewrite/reports/automated-stack-295-296-2026-09-16 and FOLLOWUP.md). It used 8 frozen synthetic scenarios with 2 editor models ([a Claude model] and opencode mimo-v2.5-free), one response per case, judged by an OpenAI-family Codex model with no human review. Cycle 3: 15/16 passed, and the gate FAILED because MiMo claimed an edit it had not made. Cycle 5: 14/16 passed; Claude deleted a source-internal imperative and MiMo omitted the final text. The report says the gate remains unsatisfied and that landing was a maintainer exception.

Editorial decision cards #206 (evals/rewrite/reports/editorial-cards-206-*). The development pilot ran 32 tasks per batch with one inherited model family and model reviewers. All 16 'keep' inputs came back byte-identical. Raw preservation flags were baseline 1 vs candidate 3 in the initial run and 2 vs 1 in the revised run. A follow-up of 16 tasks gave preservation 0/0 and missed edits 1 (pre-repair) vs 0. The final check (2026-10-18) used [a Claude model] and a GPT model via Codex CLI, 24 outputs each (8 core + 16 probes), each assessed by the other model, and found no verified failure. A third editor (Inkling) failed and invented a replacement conclusion. The report explicitly says this is not evidence of better writing quality.

Preservation policy #204. Nine validator scenarios were run on two families (Cursor composer-2.5 and [a Claude model]). Both returned PASS on two number-spelling cases even though a residual audit had been requested, which the report counts as incomplete-audit reporting failures.

Carve-out recall #140 (evals/carve-out-recall, measured at v3.39.0). It used 73 candidate strings from the repo itself, labeled by one person. The carve-outs suppressed 0 true tics. The corpus has no essays or marketing copy, so the result is limited to technical and repository text.

Historical comparative pilot #201 (evals/rewrite/README.md). It has 48 synthetic cases and 3 conditions (baseline, candidate, simple prompt) and was designed for blind human review, but the README says 'No comparative model run or human adjudication has been performed'. The repo has no evidence comparing the skill with a plain prompt, with other humanizers, with human readers' judgments, or with AI-detector outcomes.

The full example had invented resolution times, a Datadog attribution, a paying-customer count, and EMEA hiring and log-management plans. evals/rewrite/demo.json now checks the README pair with literal phrase rules.

items.rule: Trigger the skill whenever drafting, editing or reviewing prose, to remove predictable AI tells.
items.v14_evidence: SKILL.md line 8: 'Use this skill for any prose a person will read: essays, college applications, reports and papers, emails, posts, cover letters, summaries.' The description triggers on write/edit/improve/proofread/polish/humanize and 'does this sound like AI?' (Detect/review mode). v14 also adds 'Skip it for code, data tables and one-line chat answers.'

items.rule: Delete throat-clearing openers (Here's the thing, The uncomfortable truth is, It turns out, The real [X] is, Let me be clear, The truth is, I'll say it again, I'm going to be honest, Can we talk about, Here's what I find interesting, Here's the problem though) and state the content directly.
items.v14_evidence: Partly covered. tells.md S3: 'Run-ups and signposts. "Here's the thing", "Let's break this down", "In this essay I will explore", "The answer? Simple." Fix: start with the claim.' and the SKILL.md Staging row. Only 'Here's the thing' (and 'the real question' in the tells.md section 6 list) is named, so the other ten are new examples of a class v14 already has. S3 is unmarked, so v14 acts on it in aggregate; stop-slop deletes every instance. Catalog P2: the class is M (Graphite signposting), the specific openers are grade C only. DEVLOG section 1.1 already marked stop-slop's throat-clearing entries as the one part worth borrowing. Adding them as S3 examples breaks no hard rule.

items.rule: Treat any 'here's what/this/that' construction as throat-clearing: cut it and state the point.
items.v14_evidence: v14 names 'Here's the thing' (tells.md S3) but keeps a colon before a list, quote or link (R5: 'keep a colon only before a list, a quote or a link'). So 'Here's what we changed:' followed by a list survives in v14 and would be cut here. The 'any' generalization is new. The catalog has no frequency evidence for 'here's what/this/that' (P2, grade C). In a user's own draft, Edit mode would limit it to 'clear AI tells'.

items.rule: Delete emphasis crutches: 'Full stop.'/'Period.', 'Let that sink in.', 'This matters because', 'Make no mistake', 'Here's why that matters'.
items.v14_evidence: Partly covered. 'This matters because' and 'Here's why that matters' fall under tells.md S2: 'Importance flags (strong; very frequent in current Claude). "This matters because", "Why this matters:" ... Fix: give the consequence' (catalog P6: 'this matters' 116x human, M). New entries: 'Full stop.'/'Period.', 'Let that sink in.' (catalog S6, grade C only) and 'Make no mistake' (no evidence). Deleting them loses no meaning.

items.rule: Replace business jargon using a fixed table (navigate->handle, unpack->explain, lean into->accept/embrace, landscape->situation, game-changer->significant, double down->commit, deep dive->analysis, circle back->revisit, etc.).
items.v14_evidence: tells.md section 6 lists 'landscape (abstract)' and 'navigate (abstract)' under the heading 'Vocabulary (last pass; rewrite the sentence, never just swap the word)'. The other jargon (unpack, lean into, game-changer, double down, deep dive, circle back, on the same page) is new as detection entries. The fixed replacement table goes against v14's rewrite-not-swap method and against catalog O2 (a swap often replaces one overused word with another). Its 'significant' for game-changer is itself a flagged word (catalog RP2: +99% after GPT revision), and 'embrace' is stock. Import the words as detection entries only, not the swaps.

items.rule: Remove every adverb (every -ly word, all softeners, intensifiers and hedges), with no exceptions.
items.v14_evidence: Breaks hard rule 2 (SKILL.md): 'every claim, hedge and number survives unless the user agrees to cut it. Never make a claim stronger than its evidence.' Deleting every adverb removes hedges and quantity words (probably, only, nearly, rarely, approximately) and makes claims stronger. tells.md T5: 'Keep hedges that carry real uncertainty'. research.md rule 6: 'Keep a hedge the notes have'. Catalog T2 and section 12: casual qualifiers ('pretty', 'sort of', 'very', 'perhaps') are measured human signals (Graphite, M). O10 warns against stripping all hedges. DEVLOG section 1.1 already judged 'no adverbs' an over-correction.

items.rule: Delete named offender adverbs as empty emphasis: really, just, literally, genuinely, honestly, simply, actually, deeply, truly, fundamentally, inherently, inevitably, interestingly, importantly, crucially.
items.v14_evidence: Covered part: tells.md T3 'Intensifiers and sincerity markers. genuinely, truly, deeply, incredibly, absolutely, ... "honestly". Fix: delete', and SKILL.md step 4 'speech filler such as really, kind of, actually, basically, stuff' (DEVLOG section 21: 'really' 21.0 per 10,000 words in v7 against 4.7 in admitted essays). New entries: just, literally, simply, fundamentally, inherently, inevitably, interestingly, importantly, crucially. They are compatible only where they are empty emphasis. 'just' meaning only or recently, and 'inevitably' asserting necessity, carry meaning that hard rule 2 protects. Catalog evidence for the new entries is thin: 'crucial' and sentence-initial 'Importantly'/'Notably' are Kobak M but weak alone (P7).

items.rule: Cut filler phrases: 'At its core', 'In today's [X]', 'It's worth noting', 'At the end of the day', 'When it comes to', 'In a world where', 'The reality is'.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md section 6 already has "in today's fast-paced world", "it's worth noting", "it's important to note" and "the real question". New entries: 'At its core' (catalog P3: Graphite boilerplate, M but declining), 'At the end of the day', 'When it comes to', 'In a world where', 'The reality is' (no catalog evidence for these four). They are pure filler, so cutting them keeps the meaning.

items.rule: Remove self-referential asides: 'Hint:', 'Plot twist:'/'Spoiler:', 'You already know this, but', 'But that's another post'.
items.v14_evidence: Not in v14. The nearest rules are tells.md R5 ('keep a colon only before a list, a quote or a link'), which catches 'Plot twist:' in generated text, and PE10's framing devices ('(I counted)'). The catalog has no entry or frequency evidence for these blog-register asides.

items.rule: Remove the stock framings 'X is a feature, not a bug' and 'Dressed up as'.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md T4: 'Mannered prose. Metaphor performing cleverness: ... "a mirror, not a window". Fix: the literal statement.' 'a feature, not a bug' has the same shape, and 'Dressed up as' is a mannered metaphor under the same entry. tells.md S1 also covers 'X rather than Y' contrasts.

items.rule: Delete signposting and meta-joiners ('The rest of this essay explains...', 'Let me walk you through...', 'In this section, we'll...', 'As we'll see...', 'I want to explore...').
items.v14_evidence: tells.md S3: '"In this essay I will explore" ... Fix: start with the claim. (Signposting in research papers is a convention; see research.md.)' research.md keeps 'Signposting tied to content ("Section 4 reports the audit")'. Outside research writing v14 makes the same deletion. The research carve-out is deliberate (catalog RP3 and section 13 genre conventions).

items.rule: Remove performative emphasis (false intimacy or manufactured sincerity): 'creeps in', 'I promise', 'They exist, I promise'.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md T3 has the category 'Intensifiers and sincerity markers' (genuinely, honestly) but none of these phrases, and 'creeps in' is not a sincerity marker. The catalog has no frequency evidence for these phrases (V4: even 'honestly' is U as a measured tell). A real 'I promise' in a casual message is the writer's voice, and Edit mode would keep it.

items.rule: Do not announce difficulty or significance ('This is genuinely hard', 'This is what X actually looks like', 'actually matters'); demonstrate it.
items.v14_evidence: SKILL.md: 'Staging. Announcing points instead of making them: run-ups ("Here's the thing"), importance flags ("This matters because")...'. tells.md S2 lists 'This matters because' and 'This distinction matters' (strong). T3 deletes 'genuinely'. C4: 'Redundant exposition ... Fix: delete; let the example work.' Catalog P6: 'this matters' 116x human for current Claude (M).

items.rule: Delete vague declaratives that announce importance without naming the thing ('The reasons are structural', 'The implications are significant', 'The stakes are high', 'The consequences are real').
items.v14_evidence: tells.md T1: 'Significance inflation ... Fix: keep the fact, drop the verdict.' S2 covers importance flags. C1: 'A sentence that could move unchanged into another person's essay ... Fix: replace it with what only this writer knows, or delete it.' Hard rule 2: 'If you cut a sentence because it is a tell (a significance verdict, an unsourced "studies show"), say so after the text, and never put a position the writer did not take in its place.' v14 cuts these and reports the cut; stop-slop cuts without reporting.

items.rule: Replace a vague declarative with the specific thing or implication (or cut it); no requirement that the specific comes from the source.
items.v14_evidence: Breaks hard rule 1: 'use no fact, name, number ... that they or their source did not provide. A made-up specific is worse than the vague sentence it replaced.' 'Name the specific thing' with no source limit invites invented reasons and implications. v14 already has the safe form: tells.md C2 'If the writer has not supplied an instance, ask; never invent one.' and S1's '[ask: why governance?]'. Catalog C7 and O7: inventing specifics to cure vagueness is the main humanizer failure.

items.rule: Remove negation-then-assertion contrasts ('X isn't the problem. Y is.', 'not X, it's Y') by stating Y directly and dropping the negation entirely.
items.v14_evidence: Breaks hard rule 2 (keep every claim). Dropping the negation 'entirely' also deletes licensed contrasts, where X is a view someone in the text holds, and with it a claim. v14 tells.md S1 already does the safe version with a test: 'does anyone in this context actually believe X, and does rejecting X add information? If not, state Y.' (catalog S1, Peng et al. 2026: models use the construction 2.5 to 9.2x as densely as humans, and 52.8% of model uses were unneeded against 33.3% of human uses). stop-slop's own suggested fix, 'Y matters here', is the top measured Claude tell (tells.md S2; 'this matters' 116x human).

items.rule: Avoid the telegraphed reversal 'Not because X. Because Y.'
items.v14_evidence: tells.md S1: 'Corrective framing (strong). "It's not X, it's Y", ... "This isn't about X. It's about Y."', with the license test. 'Not because X. Because Y.' has the same negation-then-assertion shape, and its fragment form is S9. Catalog S1: M (strong) plus E.

items.rule: Avoid the setup/reveal 'It feels like X. It's actually Y.'
items.v14_evidence: tells.md S12: 'Staged self-correction. Stating something false in order to reverse it ... Fix: state the true version directly.' S1 also applies, and tells.md section 6 lists 'less like X and more like Y' (catalog: 105x human for a current Claude model).

items.rule: Avoid the false transformation arc 'stops being X and starts being Y'.
items.v14_evidence: Not in v14's S1 list. The closest catalog entry is S1's 'no longer X. It is Y.' (EQ-Bench regex; M for that sub-form). PE2 (tidy epiphany) covers transformation arcs in personal essays only. Compatible in Write mode; in a user's draft, apply it only as a clear tell.

items.rule: Avoid 'doesn't mean X, but actually Y'.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md S1 corrective framing ('It's not X, it's Y', 'X rather than Y') with its license test. This pattern belongs to that family, and SKILL.md step 4 already treats 'actually' as filler.

items.rule: Avoid the false distinction 'is about X but not Y'.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md S1 lists '"This isn't about X. It's about Y."'. 'is about X but not Y' is the same contrast, and the license test applies.

items.rule: Avoid the additive hedge 'not just X but also Y'.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md S1 lists 'not just X but Y' by name, and examples.md example 4 shows the fix. Catalog S1: 'not just X, but Y' appeared in 6% of GPT-4o chats (WaPo); Gemini 'is not just a _ it is' 153x (Graphite).

items.rule: Do not list what something is not before saying what it is ('Not a X... Not a Y... A Z.'); state Z.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md S1 (negation before assertion) plus S9: 'Fragment stacks and one-line punchlines. "No baseline. No audit. No accountability." ... Fix: one sentence carrying the specific claim.' Catalog S1 lists 'No X. No Y. Just Z.'

items.rule: Avoid performative-simplicity fragments '[Noun]. That's it. That's the [thing].'
items.v14_evidence: tells.md S9 (fragment stacks and one-line punchlines) and S3 ('"The answer? Simple."'). Catalog S6: grade C only.

items.rule: Avoid staccato polysyndeton fragments 'X. And Y. And Z.'
items.v14_evidence: SKILL.md Rhythm row: 'fragment stacks ("No plan. No data. No excuse.")'; tells.md S9; step 4 'choppy fragments'. DEVLOG section 21 cue coding: 'Short punchy beats' was cited as a sign of AI in 42% (plain) and 57% (word list) of ratings.

items.rule: Avoid artificial-revelation setups like 'This unlocks something. [Word].'
items.v14_evidence: SKILL.md Staging: 'Announcing points instead of making them'. tells.md S3 run-ups ('The answer? Simple.') and S9 one-line punchlines. personal-essay.md signposts ('The strange part was').

items.rule: Write complete sentences instead of emphatic fragments; trust content over presentation.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md S9: 'Fix: one sentence carrying the specific claim.' SKILL.md step 4 lists 'choppy fragments' among over-corrections. tells.md section 8: 'Chopping sentences into fragments for "burstiness". Fragment runs are a tell of their own.' v14 keeps deliberate genre exceptions: short-answers.md allows 'a fragment or a list' in very short takes, and the activity list needs 'no full sentences'.

items.rule: Avoid Socratic 'What if [reframe]?' openers.
items.v14_evidence: Not in v14, and the catalog has no evidence for 'What if' openers. Keep any rule narrow. messages.md lets an appeal open on 'the question that made the writer run ... "Did you know...?"' (from 32 real appeals), and SKILL.md's explanations note says to 'start from a question a reader actually has'. A general ban on question openers would contradict that data-based guidance.

items.rule: Delete redundant previews like 'Here's what I mean:'.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md S3: '"Here's the thing" ... Fix: start with the claim.' plus R5: 'keep a colon only before a list, a quote or a link'. 'Here's what I mean:' is the same run-up.

items.rule: Delete condescending prompts like 'Think about it:'.
items.v14_evidence: Not named in v14. It is an S3-type run-up, and R5 would drop its colon, but nothing tells the model to cut 'Think about it.' itself. No catalog evidence.

items.rule: Delete permission-granting lines like 'And that's okay.'
items.v14_evidence: personal-essay.md: 'Endings that don't: ... a deflating aside added to sound modest ("but it's okay")'. tells.md PE10: 'an ending that shrugs ("I still don't know", "but it's okay")'. DEVLOG section 21: v7 essays ended on 'but it's okay' and 'I'm fine with that'; v8's fix raised held-out p(real) by +7.5 [+2.4, +13.1]. v14 still keeps a doubt the writer really holds.

items.rule: Instead of rhetorical setups, make the point and let readers draw their own conclusions.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md C4: 'Redundant exposition ... Fix: delete; let the example work.' personal-essay.md: 'let scenes, quotes and contrasts stand without a sentence that explains them'. Catalog S5: redundant exposition was 18% of professional edits (A). v14 also guards the opposite failure, which stop-slop does not: PE9, an over-corrected essay with no reflection at all.

items.rule: Avoid the narrative template 'By the time X, I was Y.'
items.v14_evidence: Not in v14, with no catalog or DEVLOG evidence. 'By the time X, I was Y' is ordinary narrative English, and admitted essays often tell their stories in order (DEVLOG section 21). Compatible but untested.

items.rule: Replace indirect 'X that isn't Y' phrasing with a direct statement such as 'X is broken'.
items.v14_evidence: Breaks hard rule 2: 'Never make a claim stronger than its evidence.' The rule's own model turns 'X that isn't Y' into 'X is broken', a stronger and different predicate (not working well becomes broken). A neutral restatement with the same meaning would be fine, but v14 already allows that.

items.rule: Ban false agency (inanimate things taking human verbs: 'the decision emerges', 'the data tells us', 'the market rewards', 'the culture shifts').
items.v14_evidence: Not a v14 category. tells.md T4 (mannered prose) covers the figurative cases ('trust is the currency of reporting'), and R3's 'give sentences real subjects (people, the school, the writer)' applies only to repeated openers. The catalog has no frequency evidence for false agency. A ban must not touch research conventions: research.md says '"Table 2 shows" is a convention, not a tell'. The ban itself invents nothing; its fixes do (see SS36).

items.rule: Fix false agency by naming the human actor; the model example adds an actor and a time frame ('The team fixed it that week').
items.v14_evidence: Breaks hard rule 1. The model fix adds an actor ('the team') and a time frame ('that week') that 'the complaint becomes a fix' does not contain, and the table rewrites add buyers, a project and shipping. Hard rule 1 says: 'If a sentence needs a detail you lack, ask, or write [ask: ...], or write a plainer sentence.'

items.rule: If no specific person fits as the actor, use second-person 'you'.
items.v14_evidence: Breaks hard rule 2 (keep the meaning). Using 'you' as the fallback actor assigns the action to the reader ('Mistakes were made' becomes 'you made mistakes') and changes who did what. In Coach and Edit modes it also rephrases the writer's sentences (hard rules 4 and 5). Our only test of a 'you' rule found no gain: v5's 'Explainers talk to the reader ("you")' ranked 1.62 against v4's 1.50 on explainers (DEVLOG section 12) and was dropped for 'no measurable effect' (section 13, item 6).

items.rule: Avoid the narrator-from-a-distance voice ('Nobody designed this.', 'This happens because...', 'People tend to...'); put the reader in the scene.
items.v14_evidence: Breaks hard rules 1 and 2. 'You don't sit down one day and decide to...' replaces the claim 'Nobody designed this' with an imagined scene the source never gave. 'This happens because...' and 'This is why...' are how v14 explanations 'show the reasoning step by step' (SKILL.md genre notes). DEVLOG sections 12 and 13: the second-person rule had no measurable effect.

items.rule: Prefer second person over generic third person ('You' beats 'People'), and concrete specifics over abstractions.
items.v14_evidence: The 'You beats People' half was tested. v5 added 'Talk to the reader ("you") where it helps' for explainers; v4 without it ranked 1.50 against v5's 1.62 on explainers (DEVLOG section 12), and the rule was dropped for 'no measurable effect' (section 13, item 6). The 'Specifics beat abstractions' half is already in v14 with the source limit: tells.md C2 'If the writer has not supplied an instance, ask; never invent one.'

items.rule: Use active voice everywhere: every sentence needs a human subject; no passive constructions, no exceptions.
items.v14_evidence: Breaks hard rule 1: 'Every sentence needs a human subject' forces an actor where the source gives none. Our data is also against it. DEVLOG section 23: real ISEF abstracts used 1.5 passives per 100 words against 0.7 for the skill's first versions; r0's first-person advice produced half the real passive rate; r1 restored passive for procedures (research.md rule 7: 'Passive voice is normal for procedures'). tells.md section 9 lists 'passive voice' as a weak tell never acted on alone. Catalog RP5: models use agentless passives at about half the human rate.

items.rule: Rewrite passives by naming the actor and putting them first ('It is believed that' -> name who believes it; 'The decision was reached' -> name who decided).
items.v14_evidence: Breaks hard rule 1. 'Name who believes it' and 'Name who decided', with no limit to the source, make the model supply a believer or decision-maker. In v14, passive voice is a weak tell (tells.md section 9) and normal in methods (research.md rule 7). The rule would be compatible only if restricted to actors the source names, which v14's fact diff already enforces.

items.rule: Do not start sentences with What/When/Where/Which/Who/Why/How; restructure to lead with subject or verb (absolute, so it catches every question and temporal 'When').
items.v14_evidence: Breaks hard rule 2, and hard rules 4 and 5 in edits. It would turn every question (a request in an email, a reader's question in an explanation) into a statement, which changes what the sentence does, and it would rewrite a writer's ordinary 'When I was ten,'. Coach mode forbids this: 'You do not: write the essay, rewrite or rephrase its sentences' (personal-essay.md). No catalog evidence supports it, and forcing subject-first openers pushes toward the repeated-opener tell (tells.md R3, catalog S9).

items.rule: Turn Wh- cleft openers into direct statements ('What makes this hard is...' -> 'The constraint is...'), or better, name the specific constraint.
items.v14_evidence: Partly in v14: personal-essay.md bans signposts including 'What I didn't expect', and tells.md PE11 names 'signposts ("The strange part was")'. Restructuring a pseudo-cleft keeps the meaning. The 'better' path (name the specific constraint) is compatible only when the constraint comes from the source; otherwise hard rule 1 requires '[ask: ...]'. Catalog support is weak (V7, Reinhart: that-clauses as subjects 2.6x human).

items.rule: Do not start paragraphs with 'So'; start with content.
items.v14_evidence: Not in v14 (its speech-filler list is 'really, kind of, actually, basically, stuff'). No catalog evidence. Reasonable for text the model writes from spoken notes (DEVLOG section 21 on tics carried from notes into prose); Edit mode would leave a writer's own 'So' alone.

items.rule: Remove a sentence-opening 'Look,'.
items.v14_evidence: Not in v14's tells.md. The research catalog P2 lists standalone 'Look,' as a staged run-up (grade C, no frequency study). It belongs to the S3 class.

items.rule: Replace three-item lists with two items or one.
items.v14_evidence: Breaks hard rule 2: dropping list items removes claims. SKILL.md Rhythm row: 'keep list items that are distinct (often two, sometimes four)'. tells.md S8: 'Fix: keep the items that are distinct and true. Vary list lengths.' Catalog S2 found no direct frequency count of triads, and DEVLOG section 1.1 lists 'no triads' among stop-slop's over-corrections.

items.rule: Do not ask a question and answer it immediately; let it breathe or cut it.
items.v14_evidence: Partly covered: tells.md S3 lists '"The answer? Simple."', a staged question answered at once. The general ban is new and clashes with v14's own guidance (no hard rule): SKILL.md explanations 'start from a question a reader actually has', and messages.md allows a 'Did you know...?' opening. No catalog evidence for the general form.

items.rule: Vary paragraph endings; do not end paragraphs on punchy one-liners.
items.v14_evidence: SKILL.md Endings row: 'At most one or two kicker endings per piece; let most paragraphs end on their last piece of content'. Step 4 counts the last sentence of every paragraph. tells.md S11: '(strong in aggregate; the main tell that anti-AI rewrites create)'. Evidence: DEVLOG section 1.1 (issue #229: aphoristic closers rose from 38 to 61); section 23 (punchy last line in 8 of 16 plain short answers against 3 of 16 real). v14's cap is better than a ban: section 21 found 20% of real essays' paragraphs end on a short line, against 7% for v7.

items.rule: Remove every em dash; use commas or periods; the ban is absolute.
items.v14_evidence: DEVLOG section 21: real admitted essays used 0.17 dashes per 100 words, while plain, word-list and v7 essays used 0. The log says v7 moved away from real essays because 'its rules ban or discourage exactly the things these admitted students did'. Section 24 surface features: dashes alone separated real essays from model essays (AUC 0.998), so a zero-dash rule removes a human signal. v14 already avoids dashes in its own text (tells.md R6: 'Default: avoid them'), but 'A user's own drafts or style rules override this', and Edit mode keeps the writer's punctuation habits. An absolute ban would strip a writer's dashes (hard rule 4). Catalog F1 and O5: current Claude uses almost none (0.015 per 1,000 words).

items.rule: Do not stack short punchy sentences.
items.v14_evidence: SKILL.md Rhythm row: 'fragment stacks'. tells.md S9. Step 4: 'Watch for ... choppy fragments, every paragraph opening with a short punchy sentence'. DEVLOG section 21 cue coding: short punchy beats were cited as AI in 42% to 57% of ratings of plain and word-list essays.

items.rule: Avoid reassuring fragment hedges like 'Not always. Not perfectly.'
items.v14_evidence: tells.md S9 (fragment stacks). short-answers.md: 'a hedged or trailing ending ("Maybe both.", "I think.", ...)'. personal-essay.md: 'Do not balance it ... or hedge it'. DEVLOG section 23: hedges were cited in 50% to 53% of ratings of model short answers and in none of the real ones.

items.rule: Replace lazy extremes (every, always, never, everyone, everybody, nobody) with specifics.
items.v14_evidence: Breaks hard rule 1: 'Use specifics instead of sweeping claims', with no source limit, invites invented counts or examples. v14's safe form: hard rule 2 ('Never make a claim stronger than its evidence'), Rebuild ('A generalization stated as fact ... [is an error] too') and tells.md C2 ('never invent one'). In a writer's own text, replacing 'never' with a number they did not give changes the claim.

items.rule: Mix sentence lengths.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md R1: 'Uniform sentence length (strong in aggregate) ... Fix: vary length where the meaning changes pace ... Never chop at random.' Also the SKILL.md Rhythm row. DEVLOG section 22: sentence-length SD was 8.2 words in real appeals against 4.2 to 4.6 in model versions.

items.rule: Mechanical check: if three consecutive sentences have matching length, break one.
items.v14_evidence: Our real-writing benchmarks show model text is too short as well as too even, so breaking sentences up widens the length gap. DEVLOG section 21: admitted essays average 17.9 words per sentence with 11% at 30+ words (plain 13.3 and 2%). Section 23: short answers 21.8 against 11.7. Section 22: appeals 14.8 (SD 8.2) against 10.3 (SD 4.2); v9's guidance toward longer, mixed sentences was part of a release that gained +11.7 p(human) on held-out appeals. v14 R1 says 'Never chop at random', and tells.md section 8 calls 'Chopping sentences into fragments for "burstiness"' an over-correction.

items.rule: Trust readers: state facts directly; skip softening, justification and hand-holding.
items.v14_evidence: Breaks hard rule 2, which protects hedges ('every claim, hedge and number survives'). 'Skip softening, justification' drops hedges and the writer's reasons. The anti-padding half is already in v14: tells.md C7 'each sentence must add a fact, a reason or a step the reader lacks' and T5 'one hedge, on the uncertain part. Keep hedges that carry real uncertainty'.

items.rule: Rewrite any sentence that sounds like a pull-quote.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md S11 on kicker endings ('short wry, poignant or quotable line ... keep the strongest one or two'). personal-essay.md: 'Avoid ... polished epigrams built to be quoted'. T4 covers mannered prose. v14 deliberately keeps one or two strong lines and tells the writer to 'Reach once or twice'; the 'any sentence' version would remove them. DEVLOG section 21: the v8b changes, which included 'reach once or twice', raised p(real) by +6.3.

items.rule: Before delivering prose, run the 12-item quick-check list (adverbs, passive, false agency, Wh- starters, here's-what, not-X-it's-Y, matching lengths, punchy endings, em dashes, vague declaratives, distant narrator, meta-joiners).
items.v14_evidence: The checklist enforces the adverb ban (SS06, hard rule 2), the passive ban (SS40, hard rule 1), the Wh- starter ban (SS42) and the em-dash ban (SS49, contradicted by DEVLOG sections 21 and 24). v14 already has a pre-delivery check, SKILL.md step 4 'Check before returning' (fact diff, numbers, new tells, kicker count). stop-slop's list has no fact check.

items.rule: Self-score 1-10 on Directness, Rhythm, Trust, Authenticity and Density; revise below 35/50; the model judges itself.
items.v14_evidence: Not in v14, and it breaks no hard rule. Our data says model ratings favor polish: model judges rated real writing lowest on quality (DEVLOG section 21: essays 5.97 against plain 6.42; section 23: short answers 4.78 against 7.09). The author's pilot disagreed with the model judges in 6 of 6 pairs (sections 20 and 25), and section 25 lists same-family judging as a weakness. A self-score of 'Sounds human?' has no external check; v14's fact diff is the check that matters.

items.rule: Consult stop-slop's examples.md for before/after transformations to imitate.
items.v14_evidence: Breaks hard rules 1 and 2. Three of stop-slop's five examples add or drop claims: Example 1 adds 'technology is manageable', Example 2 deletes 'most', and Example 3 invents 'Move faster. Your competition is.' Imitating them teaches invention. v14's own references/examples.md fills this role: 'Every "after" uses only facts present in the "before".'

items.rule: (By example) Delete quantifiers like 'most' as 'hedging', turning qualified claims into universal ones.
items.v14_evidence: Breaks hard rule 2: 'every claim, hedge and number survives ... Never make a claim stronger than its evidence.' Deleting 'most' makes a qualified claim universal. tells.md section 8 lists 'Stripping every hedge' as an over-correction (catalog O10, T2).

items.rule: (By example) Compress a multi-clause passage to its 'core message' in a few words, even when that drops content and yields a slogan.
items.v14_evidence: Breaks hard rules 1 and 2. 'Move faster. Your competition is.' adds an imperative and a claim the input did not make, and drops discomfort, uncertainty and clarity. tells.md section 8: 'Meaning drift: rewriting so freely that claims change.' The result is also a kicker line (S11).

items.rule: (By example) Fold dramatic fragments into a single sentence (the output uses an em dash and keeps a three-item list).
items.v14_evidence: tells.md S9: 'Fix: one sentence carrying the specific claim.' Folding fragments into one sentence is already v14's fix. The example output ('Speed, quality, cost—pick two.') is itself a slogan with an em dash and a triad, a kicker under S11, so it should not be copied.

items.rule: (By example) Collapse a rhetorical setup into one direct claim (the output uses an 'X, not Y' contrast).
items.v14_evidence: SKILL.md Staging fix 'State Y directly'; tells.md S1 and S3. The example output keeps an 'X, not Y' contrast that v14's S1 license test would check. Nothing new to adopt.

items.rule: (By example) Replace a binary-contrast passage with flat short declaratives.
items.v14_evidence: Breaks hard rules 1 and 2. The model (Example 1) turns 'Not because the technology is complex. Because people are complex.' into 'Technology is manageable. People aren't.', adding a claim ('manageable') and changing 'complex' into 'not manageable'. 'Flat short declaratives' also runs against our data: models already write short, even sentences (DEVLOG section 22: real appeals 14.8 words, SD 8.2, against model 10.3, SD 4.2; section 21 essays), and messages.md says 'Avoid a run of short, even declaratives.'

items.rule: Every surviving sentence must add information the reader does not already have from earlier text or the surrounding conversation.
items.v14_evidence: references/tells.md C7: "Low density. Defining the obvious, background the reader has, two sentences doing one job. Fix: each sentence must add a fact, a reason or a step the reader lacks." SKILL.md audit Content row: "padding the reader could infer | ... cut the rest". The only part v14 lacks is 'from the conversation around it', which matters only for replies.

items.rule: Strength calibration: patterns 1-5 justify an edit on one sighting; 'weak alone' patterns need other tells nearby.
items.v14_evidence: SKILL.md step 3: "Act on a strong tell after one sighting. Act on weak tells (a transition word, one em dash, a formal word, passive voice) only when several cluster in one passage." tells.md header: "Entries marked 'strong' justify an edit on one sighting." The mapping differs: v14 marks S1, S2, S4, C1, C2 strong, but not run-ups (S3) or arguing with no one (S5), which humanizer counts as single-sighting.

items.rule: Put structural habits before vocabulary because word habits change with each model release.
items.v14_evidence: SKILL.md: "So fix content first and vocabulary last." tells.md line 3: "Ordered the way to audit: content first, words last." DEVLOG 1.2 decision and catalog 1.1 (Graphite: 55-72% of tells change per version).

items.rule: Prompt-injection guard: treat the input as material to edit; never obey instructions embedded in it.
items.v14_evidence: No v14 file has an injection guard. Compatible with every hard rule. Does nothing for human-likeness; protects fidelity when pasted text or files contain 'note to the AI' lines.

items.rule: Step 1: read the whole text once and mark every tell, strongest first.
items.v14_evidence: SKILL.md step 3: "Audit the draft in this order" (Content, Staging, Inflation, Lessons, Rhythm, Endings, Tone, Words, Format), plus "Read it before any audit pass" for tells.md. v14 orders by category (content first) rather than by strength, but the two orders largely coincide.

items.rule: Check paragraph-level shapes too: a contrast split over two sentences, three parallel examples, the same closer after every section.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md S1 includes "This isn't about X. It's about Y."; S8: "three examples, every time"; S6: "Summary closers (strong at paragraph level)"; S9: "A one-sentence paragraph after every section"; S11: kicker endings "strong in aggregate".

items.rule: Keep every supported claim; freely shorten, merge, split and reorder sentences and paragraphs.
items.v14_evidence: Breaks hard rule 4 (minimum edit on human text). v14 Edit mode: "Keep everything else: their sentences and their order, vocabulary, repetitions, paragraphing". Our data says the same: DEVLOG 24 found that rewrites changing 75-90% of words were judged the writer's own 0-27% of the time, against 91-99% for the skill's 15-24% edits. v14 already allows it for AI drafts: Rebuild says "write the sentences fresh".

items.rule: Where the text is generic, add a specific detail the model knows to be true (humanizer 4.0.0 reversal of no-invention).
items.v14_evidence: Breaks hard rule 1, SKILL.md: "use no fact, name, number, date, quote, source... that they or their source did not provide. A made-up specific is worse than the vague sentence it replaced." Also contradicted by DEVLOG 25 rg5: allowing general knowledge in school essays raised unsupported claims per text from 2.08 to 3.33, including a wrong claim about a novel, so v14 narrowed it to explanations only.

items.rule: If a sentence needs a detail the model lacks, ask the user or write a simpler sentence.
items.v14_evidence: SKILL.md hard rule 1: "If a sentence needs a detail you lack, ask, or write `[ask: what did your dad actually say?]`, or write a plainer sentence."

items.rule: Verify that no fact, name, number, date, quote, citation, ranking or simultaneity claim was dropped or changed; triads, qualifiers and list conversions are the riskiest.
items.v14_evidence: v14 has the principle (hard rule 2: "every claim, hedge and number survives unless the user agrees to cut it"), but its step-4 fact diff runs one way only. It checks output against source for additions ("list every name, number... in the output and confirm each comes from the user"). It has no input-to-output check for drops, and it does not name merges that create false simultaneity or rankings. Add the reverse check next to the additions check, not in place of it. DEVLOG 24 meaning checks still count removals (v13.1 abstracts: 0.62 removed per text).

items.rule: Read the draft aloud for leftover AI sound, then re-scan for the tells that most often survive (§1, §2, §6, §8, §19).
items.v14_evidence: v14 step 4 covers the read-through ("Read it as the target reader. Does any sentence only exist to sound good?") and a scan for NEW tells ("Did the rewrite create new tells?" plus the kicker count). It has no re-scan for tells that survived the rewrite. research/anti-ai-writing/tools/tellcheck.py could serve as that pass.

items.rule: Restate each point directly instead of patching flagged phrases one at a time.
items.v14_evidence: SKILL.md audit Words row: "Rewrite the sentence around its claim; do not just swap the word"; tells.md section 6 heading: "rewrite the sentence, never just swap the word"; Rebuild: "write the sentences fresh". In Edit mode on human text, v14 deliberately limits this to minimum edits.

items.rule: If a sentence stays awkward, rewrite the whole paragraph around its main point.
items.v14_evidence: Applied to a human's own text, this breaks hard rule 4 (minimum edit). Edit mode keeps "their sentences and their order", and Coach says "If a sentence is unclear or needs rewriting for content, explain the problem and let them rewrite it." It is compatible only inside Write or Rebuild on model-written drafts, where v14 already writes fresh.

items.rule: Vary sentence length in the final version.
items.v14_evidence: SKILL.md audit Rhythm row: "Vary length where the meaning changes pace"; tells.md R1: "Fix: vary length where the meaning changes pace... Never chop at random." v14 is stricter, because it ties variation to meaning (catalog O3). Supported by DEVLOG 22 (sentence-length SD 8.2 real vs 4.2 to 4.6 model) and DEVLOG 24 (length spread AUC 0.81 on appeals).

items.rule: If the user gives a writing sample, read it first and match its sentence length, word choice, punctuation, openings and transitions.
items.v14_evidence: v14 only says a sample OVERRIDES default style rules, and only in Edit mode ("If the user also gave a writing sample, it overrides the default style rules here, including the dash rule"). It never says to read the sample first or to MATCH its measurable features, and Write mode has no sample instruction. The catalog supports adding it (O4: "use the student's own voice samples when available"; O5: keep the student's dash rate). So does our data on surface features: dashes, colons and sentence length separate real from model essays (DEVLOG 24 surface AUC 0.997), and matching the register's punctuation gave +11.7 p (DEVLOG 22). Caveat for hard rules 1 and 3: match style only, never copy the sample's errors or facts.

items.rule: The sample overrides every pattern including the dash ban; keep dashes at the sample's rate.
items.v14_evidence: SKILL.md Edit: "If the user also gave a writing sample, it overrides the default style rules here, including the dash rule." tells.md R6: "A user's own drafts or style rules override this." v14 does not say "at the same rate" (catalog O5 does). Humanizer's "every pattern" must not extend to content rules such as invention.

items.rule: Without a sample, personal writing keeps the writer's opinions, uncertainty, humor and asides, and the model may add a reaction where the writer would.
items.v14_evidence: The keep half is already in v14 (hard rule 4: "leave strong sentences alone, including the writer's odd word choices, asides and mixed feelings"). The add half breaks hard rule 1, which bans any "feeling or memory that they or their source did not provide", and hard rule 2: "never put a position the writer did not take in its place". The plain drafts in DEVLOG 22 / LEDGER case 1 invented exactly this, a feeling and an apology.

items.rule: Reference, technical, legal and factual text stays neutral and plain.
items.v14_evidence: references/research.md rule 7: "Write in the field's register, not plain conversational English... no analogies or chatty openings"; tells.md section 8: "Register mismatch is a tell." Caution from DEVLOG 23: r0's plain-English push produced lay simplification and glossed terms, which judges cited (17% vs 4%). If imported, 'plain' must mean unadorned, not simplified.

items.rule: After the tells are removed, the result must still sound like a person, not sterile.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md section 8: "Erasing the writer's voice by polishing everything to the same smooth surface"; PE9 over-corrected essay; SKILL.md step 4: "also check the opposite failure: is there an arc and at least one line of reflection". DEVLOG 21: v8's flat or stiff register was cited as AI in 42% / 11% of ratings.

items.rule: Informal text (chats, comments, rants, angry reviews) keeps lowercase, abbreviations, fragments and emphatic stops as legitimate register.
items.v14_evidence: v14 keeps the user's punctuation in Edit ("contractions, humor and punctuation habits"; messages.md: "In the user's own text, leave their punctuation"). It has no carve-out exempting informal register from S9 fragment stacks or T3, so a model could 'fix' "Worst. Service. Ever." DEVLOG 15 names casual first-person posts as the skill's weak genre: "The skill's audit may strip the looseness these genres want." Catalog section 13 calls mixed registers an ineffective indicator.

items.rule: In informal text one tell is not enough (except chatbot residue), but two unrelated tells make the whole text a rewrite target.
items.v14_evidence: Rewriting a whole human message because of two tells breaks hard rule 4 (minimum edit). It also goes against v14's routing: "Rebuild (the user says an AI wrote it...; if you only suspect it, use Edit, since tells are not proof of authorship)". The first half (one weak tell is not enough) is already covered by SKILL.md step 3.

items.rule: Keep the writer's anger and blunt wording at full strength; do not soften.
items.v14_evidence: SKILL.md Edit: "Keep everything else: ... vocabulary"; tells.md T7: "let negative facts stay negative"; personal-essay.md: "keep it at the strength they hold it"; short-answers.md rule 4: "as strongly as the student holds them and no stronger".

items.rule: If no tell is present, return the text unchanged.
items.v14_evidence: SKILL.md hard rule 4: "If a passage is already clean, say so and return it unchanged."

items.rule: Default output for pasted text: first rewrite, list of surviving tells, final rewrite.
items.v14_evidence: As a default for any pasted text, this produces two rewrites of a human's own draft, which breaks hard rule 4 (minimum edit), and of an application essay, which breaks hard rule 5 ("You do not write the essay, rewrite or rephrase its sentences"). v14 step 5: "Return the finished text, then only what the mode or the reference calls for". The format is compatible only inside Rebuild, and there it adds nothing to the final prose.

items.rule: File mode: re-read the entire current file from disk, in chunks if long, even if the model wrote it this session.
items.v14_evidence: v14 has no file mode. The project's CLAUDE.md requires the same for the live report ("ALWAYS download and read the current version before proposing report edits"). It protects fidelity because the user edits files between turns.

items.rule: File mode: write only the final text; change prose only, leaving code, inline code, commands, paths, YAML, data and link targets untouched.
items.v14_evidence: v14 only says "Skip it for code, data tables and one-line chat answers" and gives no rule for mixed prose files (Markdown with links, YAML front matter, citations, LaTeX). Relevant to the user's paper and design-decision Markdown.

items.rule: File mode: report how many sections were reviewed and name any not covered.
items.v14_evidence: Not in v14. A transparency aid that fits CLAUDE.md's 'verify before asserting'. No effect on prose.

items.rule: Embedded mode (PRs, commit messages, documents from another task): return only the final text.
items.v14_evidence: PR and commit messages are outside v14's scope, but 'documents produced by another task' applies: CLAUDE.md routes all prose through this skill, for example from the research-paper skill. v14 step 5 does not say what to return when another skill calls it (for example, whether to drop Edit's suggestion list).

items.rule: §1 Not X but Y: state the point directly; keep a contrast only when the negative half corrects a belief the reader holds or both halves carry information.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md S1: "Test: does anyone in this context actually believe X, and does rejecting X add information? If not, state Y." examples.md #4. Catalog S1 grades this M-strong plus E (Peng et al. 2026).

items.rule: §1 variants: not just/only/merely, it's not X it's Y, X rather than Y, a contrast split across sentences, a clipped negative tail.
items.v14_evidence: Four of the five variants are in tells.md S1 ("'It's not X, it's Y', 'not just X but Y', 'X rather than Y', 'less a X than a Y', 'This isn't about X. It's about Y.'") and section 6 ("rather than merely"). Only the clipped negative tail ("..., no guessing") is missing; catalog S1 lists it but v14 does not.

items.rule: §1 applies in every language: treat the equivalent contrast construction the same way.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md S1 gives only English forms. The user writes Turkish appeals and messages (messages.md), and the main measurement of the construction is in Mandarin (catalog S1: Peng et al., 2.5-9.2x human density, 52.8% of uses unneeded).

items.rule: §2 Cut one-sentence paragraphs and stock closers that restate the previous paragraph, including the same closer after several sections.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md S6: "A last sentence restating the paragraph"; S9: "A one-sentence paragraph after every section. Fix: one sentence carrying the specific claim."; S11 kicker endings (keep the best one or two). Catalog P4 and S6 give A/M evidence; issue #229 (DEVLOG 1.1) found humanizer itself added closers.

items.rule: §2 Cut a sentence after an example, scene or number that only names what it showed.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md C4: "Redundant exposition. Telling the reader what the example just showed: 'This shows how important patience is.' ... Fix: delete; let the example work." personal-essay.md: "let scenes, quotes and contrasts stand without a sentence that explains them." DEVLOG 21: judges cited essays that "explain their own meaning".

items.rule: §2 Merge a row of dramatic fragments into one sentence with a specific claim.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md S9: "Fragment stacks and one-line punchlines. 'No baseline. No audit. No accountability.' ... Fix: one sentence carrying the specific claim." DEVLOG 21 cue coding: short punchy beats cited as AI in 42-57% of plain and word-list ratings.

items.rule: §2 Remove one-word ALL-CAPS emphasis and words separated by periods for drama (outside informal register).
