items.v14_evidence: Period-separated words are partly covered by S9 fragment stacks and T3 ("every single"). ALL-CAPS emphasis is not in v14. The catalog has no measurement for it (blader only, grade C).

items.rule: §2 Cut a closing 'Overall' or 'Ultimately' sentence that repeats a verdict the paragraph already gave.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md S6: "A last sentence restating the paragraph; 'In conclusion'; 'Ultimately,'"; research.md rule 8: "Cut ... 'Overall'". Catalog P4: Gemini "ultimately this" 78x (M).

items.rule: §2 carve-out: a short emphatic sentence may stay if it carries a new fact.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md S11 and SKILL.md step 4: "A short last sentence that simply gives the final fact, result or request is not a kicker; leave it." (v14 review point 6, DEVLOG 25).

items.rule: §3 Replace 'deep truth' framing (the real question is, at its core, fundamentally, the heart of the matter) with the specific claim.
items.v14_evidence: v14 lists only "the real question" (tells.md section 6, current-Claude list). "at its core", "fundamentally", "the deeper issue" and "heart of the matter" are not in v14 (catalog P3 has "at its core", C/M, declining). If the specific claim is not in the source, use [ask:] rather than interpret, because humanizer's own §3 examples add claims.

items.rule: §3 Replace aphorism templates (X is the Y of Z, X becomes a trap, not a tool but a mirror, the language/currency of) with a concrete statement.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md T4: "Mannered prose. Metaphor performing cleverness: 'trust is the currency of reporting', 'the quiet work of', 'load-bearing', ... 'a mirror, not a window'. Fix: the literal statement." SKILL.md Tone row. examples.md #7 keeps the meaning, where humanizer's §3 examples add claims.

items.rule: §4 Delete announcement run-ups (Let's dive in, here's what you need to know, without further ado).
items.v14_evidence: tells.md S3: "Run-ups and signposts. 'Here's the thing', 'Let's break this down', 'In this essay I will explore', 'The answer? Simple.' Fix: start with the claim." Catalog P2 (M for signposting as a class). "heads up" and "quick note" are human conventions in messages; leaving them out of v14 is fine.

items.rule: §4 Remove staged candor (a standalone 'Honestly?', 'Look', 'Real talk') before a routine claim, but leave the same words inside ordinary casual sentences.
items.v14_evidence: v14 does the opposite of the carve-out. tells.md T3 lists "honestly" as a sincerity marker with "Fix: delete", whatever its position. The catalog supports humanizer's distinction: P2 flags only the standalone "Honestly?" or "Look,", V4 notes "no frequency study for 'honestly' (U)", and section 12 counts casual qualifiers as a human signal (Graphite, M).

items.rule: §4 Replace 'the part' stand-ins (the hard part is, the part that matters) by naming the thing; leave literal parts alone.
items.v14_evidence: v14 covers this only in personal essays (tells.md PE11 "signposts ('The strange part was')"; personal-essay.md section 10 "No signposts"). General prose has no rule. DEVLOG 21: judges cited signposting in model essays ("The climb I keep thinking about was").

items.rule: §5 Remove defenses against objections nobody raised (This isn't about, I'm not saying, To be clear, Don't get me wrong).
items.v14_evidence: tells.md S5: "Arguing with no one. 'Some might argue…', 'To be clear, this isn't to say…', 'Don't get me wrong'." Catalog S8: unlicensed corrections 24.1% model vs 12.1% human (Peng et al.).

items.rule: §5 Remove fake rejected alternatives ('A tempting approach would be...', 'You might think... but').
items.v14_evidence: The mechanism is tells.md S5 ("Arguing with no one"). Those exact phrases appear in catalog S8 but not in v14's text, so a phrase list could be added to S5 at no risk.

items.rule: §5 carve-out: keep objections the text attributes or fully answers and options a reader would weigh.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md S5: "keep an objection only if a real person or source raised it (name them), or if it is the strongest objection a fair reader would raise; answer it either way." Rebuild: "Keep ... any objection a fair reader would raise".

items.rule: §6 Forced triads: check that each item is distinct; merge, develop the strongest or vary the structure; keep three only when the meaning needs three.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md S8: "Forced triads... Fix: keep the items that are distinct and true. Vary list lengths." SKILL.md Rhythm row: "keep list items that are distinct (often two, sometimes four)". Do not import "develop the strongest one" without the no-invention limit.

items.rule: §7 Repeated sentence openings: merge, change the subject or start with the action; do not ban the word; allow deliberate repetition.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md R3: "Repeated openers... Fix: merge or restructure; give sentences real subjects"; R4: "repeat the precise term"; Edit keeps the writer's "repetitions".

items.rule: §8 Hard rule: the final text contains no em or en dashes unless a sample uses them; replace each with a period, comma, colon or parentheses.
items.v14_evidence: Three DEVLOG findings go against this rule. (1) DEVLOG 21 style table: dashes per 100 words were 0.17 in real admitted essays and 0 in every model version; the skill "has ... no dashes, because its rules ban or discourage exactly the things these admitted students did". (2) DEVLOG 24 surface AUC: dashes are the strongest single feature separating real from model essays (0.998), so zero dashes marks model text. (3) DEVLOG 22: replacing dashes with colons and semicolons "pushes toward the semicolon and colon tell", fixed in v9 (+11.7 p). Catalog F1 and O5 also say do not purge to zero. Note: v14's own R6 default ("avoid them") is in tension with finding (1).

items.rule: §8 carve-out: never touch dashes or hyphens inside code, inline code, commands, paths or URLs.
items.v14_evidence: v14 skips code-only text but has no carve-out for code or URLs inside prose files. Fidelity only.

items.rule: §9 Stacked qualifiers: keep a qualifier only when the source supports it and the meaning needs it.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md T5: "Hedge stacks... Fix: one hedge, on the uncertain part. Keep hedges that carry real uncertainty"; hard rule 2: "every claim, hedge and number survives"; research.md rule 6. DEVLOG 23: hedges cited in 31-38% of model abstracts vs 6% of real ones, and in about 50% of model short answers vs 0% of real ones.

items.rule: §9 carve-out: keep scope statements, legal and safety notices and real corrections; ordinary hedges like 'perhaps' and 'tends to' are not tells.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md T5 (keep real-uncertainty hedges); section 10: "casual qualifiers in informal writing ('pretty', 'sort of')"; section 8: "Stripping every hedge" is an over-correction; SKILL.md research note: hedges in the researcher's own draft are conventions. Hard rule 2 keeps notices. "perhaps" and "tends to" are not named (catalog T2 names them).

items.rule: §10 Keep compound-modifier hyphens before the noun, drop them after it.
items.v14_evidence: Not in v14, and no catalog entry or evidence makes this a tell. DEVLOG 21 lists "wrong hyphens" among real students' errors that models do not make, so normalizing a human's hyphens moves toward model text. A true error is already fixed under Edit's outright-error rule.

items.rule: §11 Passive voice and dropped subjects: switch to active voice when that makes the actor clearer.
items.v14_evidence: DEVLOG 23 round 1: real ISEF abstracts used 1.5 passives per 100 words against 0.7 for the skill's first versions, and r0's active and first-person push read as less human. v14 research.md rule 7 now says "Passive voice is normal for procedures". Catalog RP5 (Reinhart): GPT-4o uses agentless passives at about half the human rate, so "passive voice itself is not the AI tell". Humanizer's §11 example also supplies an actor the input never named (hard rule 1). v14 already treats passive as a weak tell only.

items.rule: §12 Replace listed AI words wherever they appear; other formal words are not tells.
items.v14_evidence: The list itself is mostly in tells.md section 6. What conflicts is the 'wherever they appear' (single-sighting) trigger. DEVLOG 21: on held-out data the word-list condition was no more human than plain (+1.9 [-2.2, +6.0]; dev 48.0 vs 48.7). DEVLOG 24: surface features separate abstracts only weakly (AUC 0.77) while judges reach 1.00, so "content and structure, not word-level habits" give text away. v14 SKILL.md agrees: "swapping words does not fool them", and a formal word is a weak tell that needs a cluster. The 'other formal words are not tells' half is covered (tells.md section 9).

items.rule: §13 Drop inflated-significance phrasing (testament, pivotal moment, plays a key role, reflects a broader...) and keep the bare fact.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md T1: "Significance inflation... Fix: keep the fact, drop the verdict." SKILL.md Inflation row: "Keep the fact, drop the significance claim unless a source makes it".

items.rule: §13 Remove stock 'Challenges and Legacy / Future Outlook' sections and upbeat closers; end on the last concrete fact or on plans the source states.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md S7: "Upbeat send-offs. 'Looking ahead', 'What comes next', 'paving the way', 'The future looks bright'. Fix: state the actual next step or the limit."; T6 false balance; S6. Catalog P5: "looking ahead the" 40x, "what comes next" 24x (M). The Wikipedia-style section templates are not named, but the genre is rare for this user.

items.rule: §14 Replace vague association (associated with, linked to) with the actual relationship if known, otherwise keep the vague wording.
items.v14_evidence: 'If known' means from the model's own knowledge, which breaks hard rule 1 ("use no fact... that they or their source did not provide"). It is compatible only if 'known' is limited to what the user or source states. The fallback ("keep the vague wording") is sound and fits v14.

items.rule: §15 Cut shallow -ing add-ons unless the source supports their claim.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md S4: "'-ing' tails (strong)... Fix: cut the tail"; SKILL.md Inflation row: "', highlighting its commitment to…' tails | Keep the fact, drop the significance claim unless a source makes it". Catalog S3: Reinhart 2-5x human (M strong).

items.rule: §16 Strip ad-copy language (nestled, in the heart of, breathtaking, renowned, rich heritage, stunning) and state plainly what the thing is.
items.v14_evidence: v14 has parts of this (section 6: vibrant, groundbreaking, transformative, seamless, boast; T2 rating adjectives) but no promotional-register entry. "nestled", "in the heart of", "rich heritage", "breathtaking" and "renowned" are missing (catalog V5, M via Kobak plus WP C). Relevant to company and ESG summaries and charity appeals. The fix must restate only source facts (humanizer's examples add some).

items.rule: §17 Replace unnamed authorities with the real named source if known, otherwise cut the claim.
items.v14_evidence: Naming a source from the model's own knowledge breaks hard rule 1 ("A made-up statistic, figure, study, quote or source is never allowed"; sources only from the user). Humanizer's own example invents a 2024 NYT interview. The cut half is already covered: tells.md C6 ("name the source and what it said, or cut the claim. Never invent a source") and hard rule 2 (say so when an unsourced "studies show" is cut).

items.rule: §17 Cut prestige lists of outlets and follower counts used to prop up a person.
items.v14_evidence: Not in v14; PE4 (résumé in prose) is the nearest. Compatible if the cut is reported, as hard rule 2 requires ("If you cut a sentence because it is a tell..., say so after the text"). Mostly a Wikipedia-bio genre.

items.rule: §17 carve-out: a missing citation alone is not a tell.
items.v14_evidence: Not stated in v14. Must be scoped outside research writing, where research.md requires citations ("'Studies show' with no citation is not acceptable").

items.rule: §18 Replace copula-avoidance verbs (serves as, stands as, functions as, represents, boasts, features, offers) with is/are/has.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md section 6: "Plain-verb swaps that are always fine: serves as → is; boasts → has; utilize → use..."; SKILL.md step 2: "Use plain verbs (is, has, used, tried)." v14's list is narrower; "represents", "features" and "offers" have literal senses, so its narrower list is safer. Catalog V6 (M, Geng and Trotta).

items.rule: §19 Remove bold used as decoration (for example bolded acronyms with expansions).
items.v14_evidence: v14 covers only bold run-in labels (tells.md section 7). Scattered decorative bold is named in catalog F3 ("bold scattered for emphasis on every key term", C/A) but not in v14.

items.rule: §19 Turn a bold-label-colon bullet list into prose when the labels carry no information of their own.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md section 7: "Bold run-in labels ('**Transparency:** Transparency is…'). Turn into prose."; SKILL.md Format row. Catalog F3 (C/A; Russell formatting 15%).

items.rule: Clean formatting alone is not a tell; only decoration on every item is.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md section 7: "keep lists for real steps or parallel items"; section 9: "Genre conventions: headings, conclusions and limitations in papers; numbered steps in instructions." Catalog section 13: "The tell is decoration or formula without function."

items.rule: §20 Headings use sentence case; remove emojis and arrows from headings and list items.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md section 7: "Title Case Headings... Use sentence case" and "Emoji in anything formal. Remove." Arrows are not named.

items.rule: §20 Remove a horizontal rule between every section and a top-level heading that repeats the title.
items.v14_evidence: Not in v14; in catalog F5 (WP C). Only relevant to Markdown documents.

items.rule: §20 Rewrite headings written for effect so they name what the section contains.
items.v14_evidence: v14 only says "headings only where a reader navigates" (tells.md section 7). Clever headings are T4 mannered prose applied to headings. No measurement.

items.rule: §21 Convert curly quotes to straight where the writer or target format uses straight ones; weak alone.
items.v14_evidence: DEVLOG 21 (first design): "The real essays also had curly quotes and double spaces where the AI texts had straight ones". In our pre-2022 corpus, curly quotes marked the HUMAN texts, so treating them as an AI sign is backwards. v14 already lists curly quotes as a weak tell that needs no action alone (tells.md section 9). Matching the destination format is harmless but does nothing for human-likeness.

items.rule: §22 Strip chatbot greetings, praise, offers and sign-offs and keep the content they wrap.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md T8: "Chatbot residue. 'Great question', 'I hope this helps', 'Let me know if…', 'Certainly!'. Delete." SKILL.md step 5: "Never wrap the text in 'Here's your revised version!' or end with offers."

items.rule: §23 Replace knowledge-cutoff disclaimers (as of [date], based on available information) with a plain statement of what the source does not show, or cut them.
items.v14_evidence: Not in v14. In catalog P9 ("While specific details are limited", "based on available information"; WP 2026: among the most common current signs; mainly a GPT-6 tell). Relevant when a student pastes another chatbot's output for Rebuild. The fix ("say exactly what is missing") fits research.md's limitations rules.

items.rule: §23 Remove speculative gap-filling after an admitted lack of sources ('likely grew up...', 'it is believed that').
items.v14_evidence: SKILL.md Rebuild: "First check each of its facts, quotes and claims against the user's material: run the fact diff... A generalization stated as fact... [is an error] too"; hard rule 1. Catalog C7 documents "likely..." guesses after source hedges.

items.rule: §24 Delete a one-line opening paragraph that only restates its heading.
items.v14_evidence: Not in v14's tells.md (C4 covers examples only; C7 covers "two sentences doing one job" in general). Catalog S5 names it exactly ("a heading followed by a sentence that repeats it"; A: redundant exposition was 18% of professional edits, Chakrabarty). Common in report drafts.

items.rule: §25 Mention what a thing replaced, or a previous version, only in changelogs, release notes and migration guides.
items.v14_evidence: Aimed at code comments and technical documentation. In this user's genres (the GreenBERT report and the anti-AI paper), version history (v3 to v4 precision; v13.1 to v14) is the result itself, and cutting it would break hard rule 2.

items.rule: §25 Cut narration of how the text was compiled or sourced; keep a followable source credit and any caveat that changes what the reader should do.
items.v14_evidence: Not in v14. Must be scoped outside research methods, where research.md requires provenance ("Every number states what it was measured on, the sample size, and whether it is in-sample"). Humanizer's example adds facts ("Two vendors", "call them").

items.rule: §25 Do not describe layout or legends the reader can see ('the table below compares'); weak alone.
items.v14_evidence: Compatible only outside research writing. v14 explicitly protects the research form: SKILL.md: "Signposting ('Table 2 shows')... [is a convention], not [a tell]"; research.md: "'Table 2 shows' is a convention, not a tell."

items.rule: §26 In replies, lead with the decision and keep only the reasoning that could change whether the reader agrees.
items.v14_evidence: SKILL.md genre note: "in an email or group message that needs action, the news and the request in the first two lines"; messages.md rule 2. Cutting the user's own reasoning would break hard rule 2. The PR-reply framing is outside scope.

items.rule: §26 Leave diagnosis, evidence and proof-of-plan for the follow-up ticket or document.
items.v14_evidence: About code-review and ticket workflows, which this skill does not handle.

items.rule: §26 applies only when the surrounding conversation is visible or the text is clearly a reply.
items.v14_evidence: A scope guard for §26 (PR and review replies); not needed without H79.

items.rule: Do not edit watched phrases inside quotations, titles, proper names, or passages that discuss the phrase.
items.v14_evidence: Partly covered. tells.md section 9 has "Quotations, titles, names, and text written before late 2022." The use/mention clause (a passage that DISCUSSES a phrase) is missing from v14, though catalog section 13 has it. It matters here because the user's own anti-AI paper and LEDGER discuss "delve", "this matters" and similar phrases.

items.rule: Salutations, sign-offs and a plain 'let me know' in a message are human conventions, not chatbot residue.
items.v14_evidence: v14 is stricter. tells.md T8 lists "'Let me know if…'" as chatbot residue to delete, and examples.md #6 removes "Please let me know if you have any questions!". The refinement (delete chatbot offers to the user like "Let me know if you'd like me to...", keep a writer's own "let me know by Friday") supports hard rule 4. Salutations and sign-offs are already allowed (messages.md: "A greeting is optional"; "sign off plainly").

items.rule: Treat text written before the ChatGPT launch (30 Nov 2022) as human.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md section 9 (When not to act): "Quotations, titles, names, and text written before late 2022."

items.rule: Because judging by feel is near chance and humans absorb AI habits, require several co-occurring tells before acting on weak ones.
items.v14_evidence: The rule is in SKILL.md step 3 ("Act on weak tells... only when several cluster in one passage") and Detect mode ("patterns are evidence of generic writing, not proof of authorship"). Do not import the rationale: catalog 1.4 contradicts "little better than chance" (Russell et al.: expert annotators misclassified 1 of 300; admissions officers reached AUC 0.70).

items.rule: Preserve voice-carrying specifics: unusual concrete details and dated slang, memes and in-jokes.
items.v14_evidence: SKILL.md hard rule 4: "leave strong sentences alone, including the writer's odd word choices"; tells.md section 10: "Concrete names, dates, numbers and objects... unusual precise words"; messages.md: "the team's own name and its in-jokes if the user gave them". DEVLOG 21: odd specific details were cited as real in 88-92% of ratings.

items.rule: Preserve mixed feelings, unresolved tension, first-person choices, genuine asides, parentheticals and self-corrections.
items.v14_evidence: SKILL.md hard rule 4: "including the writer's odd word choices, asides and mixed feelings"; tells.md section 10: "parenthetical asides... mixed feelings and unresolved questions"; PE2: "keep whatever is really unresolved"; S12 allows a real self-correction once. DEVLOG 21: digressions and unevenness were cited as real in 51% of ratings.

items.rule: (Reader-flagged) Adopt humanizer's before/after examples (§2, §3, §4, §6, §11, §12, §13, §15, §17, §25, §26, README Lisbon).
items.v14_evidence: The reader found added facts in at least 14 examples (for example the Haolai River's 15 cm width, a 2024 NYT interview, Next.js cache layers, a hash map with O(1) lookups, 'two vendors'). These break hard rule 1. v14 examples.md promises "Every 'after' uses only facts present in the 'before'", and v14 review point 4 (DEVLOG 25) already removed examples of this kind. Borrow pattern names only, never the example text.

items.rule: (Reader finding) Detector tricks: none in humanizer; its README disclaims detector evasion.
items.v14_evidence: Matches v14 hard rule 3 ("No tricks. No deliberate typos, no swapped-in rare synonyms, no slang to sound casual, no invisible characters or look-alike letters") and tells.md section 8 ("Editing to a detector score"). Humanizer's 'Vary sentence length' and its dash and curly-quote rules are style rules, not burstiness targets.

items.rule: Act as a human editor who keeps the user's point and voice while making the prose clearer and livelier.
items.v14_evidence: SKILL.md description: "Edits the user's own text minimally and keeps their voice"; SKILL.md hard rule 2: "When editing, every claim, hedge and number survives unless the user agrees to cut it." The one part v14 lacks, the goal of making prose "more alive", should not be copied. DEVLOG 24 found that answering "improve it" with a rewrite changed 75-90% of words and read as AI (0-27% judged the writer's own).

items.rule: Remove AI patterns without turning distinctive writing into generic polished prose.
items.v14_evidence: references/tells.md section 8: "Erasing the writer's voice by polishing everything to the same smooth surface." SKILL.md hard rule 4: "leave strong sentences alone, including the writer's odd word choices, asides and mixed feelings."

items.rule: Trigger when the user wants a draft clearer, more direct, more opinionated or less AI-sounding, or asks if writing reads as AI.
items.v14_evidence: SKILL.md description: "Use when the user asks to write, edit, improve, proofread, polish or humanize prose ... or says \"make this sound less like AI\", \"humanize this\" or \"does this sound like AI?\"". The only trigger v14 lacks is "more opinionated". Read literally, it invites adding opinions, which hard rule 1 forbids, so it should not be copied.

items.rule: Edit is the default mode: make the minimum effective edit and return the edited draft plus a What changed section.
items.v14_evidence: SKILL.md Edit: "Minimum effective edit, even when they say \"improve it\""; SKILL.md routing: "If the user's text is their own draft, use Edit". The rule is backed by DEVLOG 24/25: v13.1 beat plain by +32 to +48 p on "improve it". The output differs: v14 lists suggested changes, not changes made. That part is judged under R64.

items.rule: In Detect mode (audit/scan/flag/'is this slop?'), name each pattern found, quote the line, and give a few-word fix.
items.v14_evidence: SKILL.md Detect / review: "Quote the passages, name the pattern, give a one-line fix." references/examples.md #10 shows the same format.

items.rule: In Detect mode do not rewrite, do not score the draft, and do not guess whether AI wrote it, because detectors only guess.
items.v14_evidence: SKILL.md Detect: "Do not guess whether a human or a model wrote it: patterns are evidence of generic writing, not proof of authorship." SKILL.md Integrity: "AI detectors are unreliable in both directions". v14 has no explicit "no score" line, but an AI-likeness score is an authorship guess, which the sentence above already forbids.

items.rule: After a Detect report, offer to edit the draft.
items.v14_evidence: Breaks no hard rule, but it reverses SKILL.md step 5: "Never wrap the text in \"Here's your revised version!\" or end with offers." tells_catalog P1 lists closing offers ("Would you like me to...") as chatbot residue. It has no effect on the prose.

items.rule: If no draft was provided, ask the user to paste it.
items.v14_evidence: v14 does not say it; the nearest is Write: "If the user gave no facts and the genre needs them..., ask two or three targeted questions first." Any model already does this, and it does not affect the prose.

items.rule: If audience or format is unclear, ask a single question about who it is for and where it will be published.
items.v14_evidence: SKILL.md step 1: "Before writing, answer four questions (silently unless the user needs to supply something): who reads this, what they should think or do afterwards, the one main point..."

items.rule: If the goal is unclear, ask what the reader should think, feel or do afterwards.
items.v14_evidence: SKILL.md step 1: "who reads this, what they should think or do afterwards ... (silently unless the user needs to supply something)".

items.rule: Before editing, note the draft's vocabulary, cadence, bluntness, humor, uncertainty, digressions and polish level, and keep the personal traits.
items.v14_evidence: SKILL.md Edit: "Keep everything else: their sentences and their order, vocabulary, repetitions, paragraphing, contractions, humor and punctuation habits." Hard rule 4: "odd word choices, asides and mixed feelings". Hard rule 2 keeps hedges. v14 keeps more than this list, with no separate noticing step.

items.rule: Do not even out paragraphs or rewrite distinctive lines just for consistency.
items.v14_evidence: SKILL.md Edit keeps "paragraphing". Hard rule 4: "leave strong sentences alone". tells.md section 8: "polishing everything to the same smooth surface".

items.rule: Minimum effective edit: fix AI patterns, errors, repetition and unclear passages only, and leave strong human sentences untouched.
items.v14_evidence: SKILL.md hard rule 4: "Fix what is broken; leave strong sentences alone". Edit: "Fix outright errors ... and anything that blocks the meaning. Cut clear AI tells if the text has them." One deliberate difference: v14 keeps "repetitions" (Edit), and tells.md section 10 counts "repeating the right word" as a human signal, so "fix repetition" should not be copied.

items.rule: A rough draft with a real voice must still sound like the same person after the edit.
items.v14_evidence: SKILL.md Edit: "For a writer whose first language is not English, fix the grammar but do not make the phrasing sound native." Description: "keeps their voice". DEVLOG 25 measured voice kept at 8.8-10 for v13.1 edits.

items.rule: Lead with the point when the setup adds nothing, cutting generic throat-clearing.
items.v14_evidence: SKILL.md step 2: "Start with the first real claim, scene or result." tells.md S3: "Here's the thing"... "Fix: start with the claim." In Edit mode v14 cuts run-ups as clear tells and leaves reordering as a suggestion.

items.rule: Keep personal asides, stories or admissions that create context, tension or character.
items.v14_evidence: SKILL.md hard rule 4: "including the writer's odd word choices, asides and mixed feelings". tells.md section 10: "small true anecdotes ... parenthetical asides ... mixed feelings and unresolved questions".

items.rule: Front-load conclusions only where it helps clarity, and don't force every unit into a point-detail-background template.
items.v14_evidence: v14 guards structure only by genre or by size: tells.md R2 ("Every paragraph four sentences. Fix: let length follow content"), PE11 engineered essay (personal essays), messages.md ("Do not build every appeal from the same parts in the same order"). Nothing forbids giving every paragraph the same point-first shape in reports or posts. In our data, tidy structure is the most cited model sign: DEVLOG 21 (75-86% of AI-essay ratings; v8b's looser-structure rule cut it to 51%), 22 (tidy plan 50-59% vs 12% real), 23 (tidy arc 35-46% vs 25%).

items.rule: Keep the user's meaning: never invent claims, examples, stats or opinions, and ask when something is unclear.
items.v14_evidence: SKILL.md hard rule 1: "use no fact, name, number, date, quote, source, anecdote, feeling or memory that they or their source did not provide... If a sentence needs a detail you lack, ask, or write `[ask: ...]`". Hard rule 2: "Keep the meaning."

items.rule: Open the writing up without dumbing it down, keeping substance, nuance and precision.
items.v14_evidence: SKILL.md hard rule 2: "every claim, hedge and number survives". research.md rule 7: "Write in the field's register, not plain conversational English. Technical terms stay technical". This is backed by DEVLOG 23, where simplification was read as AI.

items.rule: Strip only readability obstacles: jargon, long sentences, abstract nouns and tangled structure.
items.v14_evidence: DEVLOG 21 style features: real admitted essays have longer sentences than every model version (17.9 vs 11.5-15.5 words; 30+ word sentences 11% vs 1-4%) and more abstract nouns (2.9 vs 1.0-1.2 per 100 words). DEVLOG 23: r0's plain-English push produced simplification and glossed terms that judges cited as AI (17% and 10-15% vs 4% and 0% for real) and left abstracts slightly less human than plain (-3.8). Real abstracts average 23 words per sentence, some over 40. v14 research.md encodes the opposite: "Technical terms stay technical"; "do not chop it into short sentences".

items.rule: Use active voice with a doer as subject.
items.v14_evidence: DEVLOG 23: real ISEF abstracts used 1.5 passives per 100 words vs 0.7 for the skill's first versions, and r1 restored passive in procedures. v14 research.md rule 7: "Passive voice is normal for procedures". tells.md section 9 calls passive voice a weak tell. tells_catalog RP5: GPT-4o uses agentless passives at about half the human rate. The rule's example ("The team shipped it Tuesday") also supplies an actor and a day, a hard rule 1 risk.

items.rule: Never give inanimate subjects human verbs (absolute ban on personification).
items.v14_evidence: Hard rule 4 (minimum edit): an absolute ban forces rewrites of correct, conventional sentences in a human's text ("Table 2 shows", "the report claims"). SKILL.md genre notes call "Signposting (\"Table 2 shows\")" a convention, not a tell. Hard rule 1: giving the verb a human subject often means naming a doer the text never names. The legitimate target, decorative personification, is already covered by tells.md T4 mannered prose ("Fix: the literal statement"). The catalog has no measured evidence that personification is a tell.

items.rule: Make every sentence earn its place by cutting empty qualifiers and throat-clearing.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md C7: "each sentence must add a fact, a reason or a step the reader lacks." tells.md S3 run-ups, T3 intensifiers. SKILL.md step 4: "Does any sentence only exist to sound good?"

items.rule: Keep hedges such as 'I think', 'maybe' and 'to be honest' when they express real uncertainty, self-awareness or spoken rhythm.
items.v14_evidence: SKILL.md hard rule 2: "every claim, hedge and number survives". tells.md T5: "Keep hedges that carry real uncertainty". Section 10: "casual qualifiers in informal writing". This holds for the user's own draft. When writing from notes, v14 drops spoken tics (messages.md rule 8), backed by DEVLOG 22 ("bence" in 0% of real texts vs 25-31% of model texts) and DEVLOG 21.

items.rule: Split sentences or paragraphs only when they are genuinely hard to follow.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md R1: "Never chop at random." Section 8: "Chopping sentences into fragments for 'burstiness'." SKILL.md Edit fixes only "anything that blocks the meaning". research.md rule 3: "do not chop it into short sentences".

items.rule: Keep long spoken sentences, fragments and pace changes when clear and characteristic of the writer.
items.v14_evidence: SKILL.md Edit: "Keep everything else: their sentences and their order..." Hard rule 4: "leave strong sentences alone".

items.rule: Be concrete: names, numbers, dates, mechanisms and examples beat abstractions.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md C2: "Fix: the actual instance the writer has ... If the writer has not supplied an instance, ask; never invent one." v14 adds a limit from DEVLOG 23 (short-answers.md: "Do not stack numbers, ages and labels to look specific"). Do not copy no-ai-slop's examples, which invent numbers.

items.rule: Portability test: a sentence that could move unchanged to another person, company, country or product is filler. Cut it, or replace it with a subject-specific fact, example, mechanism, consequence or judgment.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md C1: "Portability (strong). A sentence that could move unchanged into another person's essay or another company's report says nothing... Fix: replace it with what only this writer knows, or delete it." v14 credits no-ai-slop for the test. Its "or a judgment" replacement path is absent from v14 and would add an opinion (hard rule 1).

items.rule: Show, don't tell: cut commentary labeling a point important, surprising, subtle or obvious, and trust the reader when the prose already shows it.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md S2: "This matters because", "This distinction matters"... "Fix: give the consequence". C4: "Telling the reader what the example just showed... Fix: delete; let the example work."

items.rule: Protect useful specific details rather than smoothing them into generic importance.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md T1: "Fix: keep the fact, drop the verdict." Hard rule 4 keeps odd word choices. tells.md section 10: "Concrete names, dates, numbers and objects". examples.md #3 keeps the ammonia-and-bleach detail.

items.rule: Replace weak verb phrases (nominalizations) with direct verbs.
items.v14_evidence: DEVLOG 21 (dev set): abstract nouns (-tion, -ness, -ity) per 100 words: real 2.9, plain 1.2, word list 1.0, v7 1.0. Current Claude output already sits at about a third of the human rate, so a denominalizing pass moves it further away. In Edit it would also change a human's wording (v14 keeps "vocabulary"). The write-side habit is already in SKILL.md step 2: "Use plain verbs (is, has, used, tried)", plus the tells.md section 6 swaps. tells_catalog V7 (Reinhart) points the other way for model text in general.

items.rule: Before structure or word choice, establish the piece's purpose and audience.
items.v14_evidence: SKILL.md step 1: "Before writing, answer four questions ...: who reads this, what they should think or do afterwards, the one main point..."

items.rule: Keep the writer's strong opinions, bluntness, humor, profanity, self-interruptions and admissions, and do not swap in safer or more professional wording.
items.v14_evidence: SKILL.md Edit: keep "vocabulary ... humor and punctuation habits"; "do not make the phrasing sound native". Hard rule 2: every claim survives, so softening a blunt claim is barred. tells.md T7: "let negative facts stay negative."

items.rule: Keep the writer's structure, progression and detours unless they hurt the piece, and justify any reorganization in What changed.
items.v14_evidence: SKILL.md Edit: "Keep everything else: their sentences and their order ... paragraphing". Bigger changes such as "the order of paragraphs" go into the list "without writing the new sentences for them". v14 is stricter: it never reorganizes, it only suggests.

items.rule: Ban outright 26 items: delve, foster, leverage, utilize, facilitate, empower, streamline, robust, cutting-edge, paradigm shift, game changer, this is huge, this changes everything, tapestry, realm, beacon, multifaceted, meticulous, intricate, paramount, transformative, elevate, embark, supercharge, harness, ever-evolving.
items.v14_evidence: DEVLOG 8 defines condition L as the "avoid delve, tapestry, em dashes" word-list approach. DEVLOG 15 (held-out): v4 ranked above the word list in 43 of 48 judgments (mean rank 1.92 vs 4.17). DEVLOG 21 (held-out vs real essays): word list vs plain +1.9 p(real) [-2.2, +6.0], so no reliable gain. DEVLOG 1.1: word lists are weak (lift 0.9). tells_catalog O6 and Antislop: bans backfire. An outright ban would also hit senses that tells.md section 9 protects (robust in statistics, foster care) and force non-error edits to a human's text. Words v14 lacks (empower, streamline, cutting-edge, paramount, elevate, harness...) could join the classic list as rewrite targets.

items.rule: Cut 11 often-empty adverbs (just, literally, honestly, simply, actually, truly, fundamentally, importantly, crucially, inherently, inevitably) when empty. Keep them when they carry emphasis, uncertainty, contrast or spoken rhythm.
items.v14_evidence: Partly covered. tells.md T3 has "truly" and "honestly"; SKILL.md step 4 and personal-essay.md cover "actually" as speech filler. Just, literally, simply, fundamentally, importantly, crucially, inherently and inevitably are not listed. The keep-condition matches tells.md section 9 (act on weak tells only in clusters). The catalog has measured evidence only for crucial and importantly (V1, P7); the rest are unmeasured.

items.rule: Cut 16 often-empty phrases when they delay the point: it's worth noting, it's important to note, at the end of the day, when it comes to, at its core, in today's world, in the age of, in the world of, the reality is, the truth is, in terms of, with regard to, in order to, going forward, in this article, let's dive in. Keep an occasional one that belongs to the writer's voice.
items.v14_evidence: Partly covered. tells.md section 6 has "it's important to note", "it's worth noting" and "in today's fast-paced world"; S3 run-ups cover "let's dive in"-type openers. The rest are new. Caution: tells_catalog section 12 lists "in order to" as a human-signal construction (WP), so it should not be a cut target. "at its core" has measured but declining evidence (catalog P3).

items.rule: Binary contrasts ('not X, it's Y', 'not just X but Y'): state Y directly.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md S1: "Corrective framing (strong)... Test: does anyone in this context actually believe X, and does rejecting X add information? If not, state Y." v14 adds a licence test (Peng et al.). Note that no-ai-slop's own fix ("The eval matters more than the model") uses "matters more than", a measured Claude tell (catalog V2, 93x).

items.rule: Cut throat-clearing openers and state the point.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md S3: "Run-ups and signposts. \"Here's the thing\", \"Let's break this down\"... Fix: start with the claim."

items.rule: Cut faux-insight setups ('what most people get wrong', 'here's what nobody tells you') and let the claim stand alone.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md S5: "Arguing with no one... Fix: keep an objection only if a real person or source raised it". tells.md S3 run-ups: "Fix: start with the claim." Current-Claude list: "the real question".

items.rule: Rewrite colon reveals (noun phrase + colon + dramatic reveal) as plain sentences, and reserve colons for lists, labels and quotes.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md R5: "keep a colon only before a list, a quote or a link". The SKILL.md Format row says the same. Backed by DEVLOG 22 (colons 0.06 per text real vs 0.38-0.47 model) and DEVLOG 24 (colons AUC 0.98 on essays).

items.rule: Prefer sentence case after a colon unless grammar, a proper noun, a title or code requires otherwise.
items.v14_evidence: v14 is silent. The catalog has no evidence that capitals after a colon are a tell. v14 already limits colons to lists, quotes and links (tells.md R5). In Edit mode this rule would change a human's correct style (APA capitalizes full sentences after a colon).

items.rule: Cut superficial-analysis trailing -ing clauses (highlighting, underscoring, reflecting, showcasing).
items.v14_evidence: tells.md S4: "\"-ing\" tails (strong). A clause tacked on to interpret the fact... Fix: cut the tail". SKILL.md Inflation row: ", highlighting its commitment to…". Do not copy no-ai-slop's example, which invents a user benefit.

items.rule: Replace importance puffery (testament, pivotal moment, vital role, solidifies its position, underscores its significance) with the plain fact.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md T1: "Significance inflation. \"marked a pivotal moment\", \"a testament to\"... Fix: keep the fact, drop the verdict." No-ai-slop's example invents a fact ("first paid product").

items.rule: Cut interpretive metadiscourse that tells the reader what to notice or how to weigh it ('The key point is', 'As you can see', 'This distinction matters', redundant 'In other words').
items.v14_evidence: tells.md S2 ("This distinction matters", "is key to"), C4: "Telling the reader what the example just showed... Fix: delete". C7: "two sentences doing one job". S3 run-ups.

items.rule: If such an aside can't just be deleted, replace it only with support or facts already in the content.
items.v14_evidence: SKILL.md hard rule 2: "never put a position the writer did not take in its place". tells.md S1: "If the sentence then needs its reason, use the writer's, or ask".

items.rule: For weasel attribution ('experts agree', 'studies show'), name the source or cut the claim, and ask the user rather than invent a source.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md C6: "Fix: name the source and what it said, or cut the claim. Never invent a source." research.md: "write `[cite: source for X]`".

items.rule: Replace fake-strong verbs (serves as, acts as) with plain 'is'/'has' when clearer.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md section 6: "Plain-verb swaps that are always fine: serves as → is; boasts → has". No-ai-slop's example invents three features.

items.rule: Avoid synonym cycling: repeat the right word instead of rotating terms.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md R4: "Elegant variation... Fix: repeat the precise term." SKILL.md step 2: "Name things precisely and keep using the same name."

items.rule: Replace negative listing ('Not a X. Not a Y. A Z.') with a plain statement of Z.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md S1 ("This isn't about X. It's about Y." ... "If not, state Y") and S9: "Fragment stacks... Fix: one sentence carrying the specific claim."

items.rule: Replace dramatic fragmentation with complete sentences.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md S9: "Fix: one sentence carrying the specific claim." SKILL.md step 4 over-corrections: "choppy fragments". Backed by DEVLOG 21 cue coding: short punchy beats were cited as AI in 42% (plain) and 57% (word list) of ratings.

items.rule: Avoid repeated sentence shapes, identical paragraph structures and stacked punchy fragments, and vary shape only when it serves the point.
items.v14_evidence: SKILL.md Rhythm row: "Runs of same-length sentences; every paragraph the same size; triads; sentence openers repeating...; fragment stacks" → "Vary length where the meaning changes pace". tells.md R3: "Fix: merge or restructure".

items.rule: Drop rhetorical setups and self-answered question pairs.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md S3: "Run-ups and signposts. ... \"The answer? Simple.\" Fix: start with the claim."

items.rule: Delete fake-profound kicker lines outright (no better metaphor, no preserved rhythm) and end on the clearest concrete sentence already present.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md S11: "keep the strongest one or two; end the other paragraphs on their last piece of content". T4: "Fix: the literal statement." C1 deletes portable lines. v14's allowance of one or two kickers is supported by DEVLOG 21: real essays end 20% of paragraphs on a short line vs 7% for v7.

items.rule: If the ending then needs closure, add a plain takeaway or next action.
items.v14_evidence: Breaks hard rule 1 (no invented opinion or recommendation) and hard rule 2: "never put a position the writer did not take in its place". SKILL.md Edit: do not add "reasons the writer did not write". v14's alternative is tells.md S6 "end on the last new point" and S7 "state the actual next step or the limit", both taken from the source.

items.rule: Cut summary-recap endings ('In conclusion', 'Ultimately', 'Overall', restating paragraph) and end on the last concrete point, takeaway or next action.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md S6: "Summary closers... \"In conclusion\"; \"Ultimately,\"... Fix: end on the last new point... A required conclusion must still do new work." v14 keeps genre limits that the blanket rule lacks: tells.md section 9 ("conclusions and limitations in papers") and short-answers.md ("End on the plain conclusion"). DEVLOG 23 found that admitted short answers "often end on a plain summary line".

items.rule: Remove formatting slop: emoji headings, mid-sentence bold, bullets that should be prose, and headers over two-sentence sections. Format follows content.
items.v14_evidence: Mostly covered by tells.md section 7: "Bullets where an argument belongs", "Emoji in anything formal", "a heading every 100 words... headings only where a reader navigates". Bold sprinkled mid-sentence for emphasis is not listed (only "Bold run-in labels"). tells_catalog F3 gives C/A evidence for overused boldface (WP; Russell formatting 15%).

items.rule: Em dashes: none in short copy, at most 1-2 in longer drafts when clearly better, and remove clusters and decorative dashes.
items.v14_evidence: Avoidance is covered by tells.md R6: "Default: avoid them... A user's own drafts or style rules override this." New is the allowance of 1-2 dashes in longer drafts, which our data support: DEVLOG 21 found 0.17 dashes per 100 words in real essays and 0 in every model version, and DEVLOG 24 found dashes the strongest single surface feature separating real from model essays (AUC 0.998). The rule must not strip a user's own dashes (hard rule 4; messages.md: "In the user's own text, leave their punctuation").

items.rule: Read the full draft before editing.
items.v14_evidence: Not stated in v14, though Rebuild implies it ("First check each of its facts"). A model does it anyway, with no effect on the prose.

items.rule: Identify the core point and the voice traits to preserve, and ask the user if the core point can't be identified.
items.v14_evidence: SKILL.md step 1: "the one main point ... (silently unless the user needs to supply something)... If the material is thin, ask for it before drafting." In Edit, v14 lists "an unclear claim" among the suggested changes. Voice traits: see R11.

items.rule: For a detect request, return the findings report and stop.
items.v14_evidence: SKILL.md Detect: "Quote the passages, name the pattern, give a one-line fix." Step 5: "Never ... end with offers."

items.rule: After a minimal edit, self-check the result against eval.md.
items.v14_evidence: v14 Edit has no check step. Write says "Run the full procedure" and Rebuild says "run the fact diff (step 4)", but Edit names neither. A short post-edit meaning check (same claim, hedge, number and strength per sentence) targets the residual measured in DEVLOG 25: v13.1 "improve" edits changed 0.50 statements per abstract and 1.06 per learner essay. It also addresses catalog O7 (meaning drift). Adopt the meaning-check items only; eval.md's active-voice and banned-word checks are contradicted (R69, R70).

items.rule: If any check fails, fix the draft and re-run the checks (loop until pass).
items.v14_evidence: SKILL.md step 4 says to fix failures ("Remove or bracket anything that does not"; rewrite extra kickers) and asks "Did the rewrite create new tells?", but has no explicit re-run loop. The loop is compatible if bounded. An unbounded loop on a human's text risks over-editing (tells.md section 8).

items.rule: Output the full edited draft plus a short What changed section.
items.v14_evidence: v14 Edit returns the text plus "up to five bigger changes the writer could make". Changes made are reported only when a tell sentence was cut (hard rule 2: "say so after the text"); Coach already returns "the list of those fixes". A short list of changes made is compatible within step 5's "few lines" and lets the writer verify meaning. It does not change the prose.

items.rule: Run eval.md after the rewrite, answering each check pass/fail, and fix before returning if any fails.
items.v14_evidence: SKILL.md step 4: "Check before returning. Fact diff: ... confirm each comes from the user or the source. Remove or bracket anything that does not." This is followed by the numbers, target-reader, new-tells and kicker-count checks. Write and Rebuild run it.

items.rule: Check that the edit adds no claims, examples, stats, quotes or opinions (adds 'quotes' to SKILL.md's list).
items.v14_evidence: SKILL.md hard rule 1 includes "quote" and "source". Edit: "Do not add transitions..., definitions, examples, statistics, appeals to authority... or reasons the writer did not write". Step 4 fact diff: "name, number, date, quote and claim".

items.rule: Keep cutting proportional to the actual slop, with no aggressive compression that strips character.
items.v14_evidence: SKILL.md hard rule 4: "Minimum effective edit... If a passage is already clean, say so and return it unchanged." tells.md section 8: "Erasing the writer's voice".

items.rule: Require concrete facts and direct verbs only where the draft supports them.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md C2: "If the writer has not supplied an instance, ask; never invent one." Hard rule 1: "A made-up specific is worse than the vague sentence it replaced."

items.rule: Active voice with human subjects 'where possible' (softer than SKILL.md's 'Never').
items.v14_evidence: DEVLOG 23: real abstracts 1.5 passives per 100 words vs 0.7 for the skill's first versions. The fix (r1) was passive voice in procedures, and active voice is "possible" there too, so the softer wording still pushes the wrong way. v14 research.md rule 7: "Passive voice is normal for procedures". tells_catalog RP5: passive voice itself is not the AI tell.

items.rule: Remove banned words, filler phrases, empty adverbs and inflated claims unless they are quoted as examples.
items.v14_evidence: The banned-word check rests on the word-list approach that DEVLOG 15 (v4 above the word list in 43 of 48 held-out judgments) and DEVLOG 21 (word list vs plain +1.9 [-2.2, +6.0] p(real) against real essays) found weak. The inflated-claims part is covered by tells.md T1, and the quotation carve-out by tells.md section 9: "Quotations, titles, names".

items.rule: Metadiscourse check widens to authorial metacommentary, reader guidance, emphasis markers and redundant glossing.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md S2, S3, C4 and T3. research.md: "Simplify for a lay reader... glosses in parentheses". v14 deliberately keeps one kind of reader guidance that this check would cut: research.md "Signposting tied to content (\"Section 4 reports the audit\")" and SKILL.md "\"Table 2 shows\"... conventions, not tells".

items.rule: When puffery or weasel attribution has no source, flag it for the user rather than fill it in.
items.v14_evidence: SKILL.md hard rule 2: "If you cut a sentence because it is a tell (a significance verdict, an unsourced \"studies show\"), say so after the text". tells.md C6: "Never invent a source." S4: "`[ask: against what target?]`".

items.rule: Final read: the writer must recognize the edited draft as their own voice.
items.v14_evidence: SKILL.md description: "keeps their voice". Edit keeps vocabulary, humor and punctuation. personal-essay.md critique item 8: "Voice: ... Ask a friend: \"does this sound like me?\"". DEVLOG 25 measured voice kept at 8.8-10.

items.rule: Final read-aloud test: the draft must sound natural read to a sharp colleague.
items.v14_evidence: SKILL.md step 4: "Read it as the target reader. Does any sentence only exist to sound good?" Caution: a sounds-natural-spoken criterion leans toward the talking register that DEVLOG 21 found hurt (casual filler cited as AI in 43% of v7 ratings; v8's written voice gained +7.5 p(real) held-out), and toward the fluency that DEVLOG 23 found most cited for model abstracts (83-96%).

items.rule: README advertises a satire mode that generates maximal AI slop on a topic. SKILL.md contains no instructions for it, so the feature is unbacked by the installed skill.
items.v14_evidence: A satire feature that generates slop, with no instructions in the installed skill. It is outside the formats we handle and has no bearing on human-likeness or fidelity.

items.rule: Flag a pattern only when several tells co-occur; a lone em dash, 'crucial', triad, curly quote or tidy sentence is not evidence.
items.v14_evidence: SKILL.md step 3: "Act on a strong tell after one sighting. Act on weak tells (a transition word, one em dash, a formal word, passive voice) only when several cluster in one passage." tells.md section 9: "One weak tell alone: a transition word, one dash, passive voice, formal vocabulary, curly quotes." All of G01's examples are weak tells in v14. One difference, deliberate: v14 still acts on one sighting of a strong tell (S1 corrective framing, S2 importance flags, S4 -ing tails), which have measured rates in the catalog (S1, S3, P6). Taking G01 wholesale would weaken that.

items.rule: Clean spelling, correct punctuation and a consistent Oxford comma are not evidence of AI.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md section 8: "Adding typos or grammar errors. Lowers quality; perfect grammar is not an AI sign." The Oxford comma is not named (trivial). Supported by DEVLOG 21 round 2 and 23 round 2: real texts with errors fixed were still judged 100% human.

items.rule: Never rewrite watched phrases inside quotations, block quotes, titles, headings, code or quoted examples.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md section 9: "Quotations, titles, names, and text written before late 2022." SKILL.md: "Skip it for code, data tables and one-line chat answers." Small gaps: words inside headings, and use-mention examples (a word discussed, not used), which catalog section 13 has but v14 tells.md lacks.

items.rule: Keep repeated technical terms exactly; do not vary jargon for elegance.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md R4: "Renaming the same thing each time... Fix: repeat the precise term." SKILL.md step 2: "Name things precisely and keep using the same name." research.md: "Domain terms ... each defined once. One concept, one name."

items.rule: Plain neutral reference/encyclopedic prose is the right human voice for that genre; not a defect.
items.v14_evidence: v14 protects academic conventions (research.md: "Academic prose has conventions that look like AI tells out of context. Keep the conventions") but says nothing about encyclopedic or reference prose. Its explanations note leans the other way ("A sequence of textbook definitions is what reads as machine-made"). Breaks no hard rule, but our users rarely write this genre.

items.rule: For samples under ~40 words, decline to score.
items.v14_evidence: v14 never scores authorship at all. SKILL.md Detect: "Do not guess whether a human or a model wrote it: patterns are evidence of generic writing, not proof of authorship."

items.rule: Low sentence-length variance alone must not raise the score.
items.v14_evidence: SKILL.md Detect: "Do not guess whether a human or a model wrote it: patterns are evidence of generic writing, not proof of authorship." Edit mode keeps "their sentences and their order".

items.rule: Formal or non-native register is not proof of AI (Liang et al.).
items.v14_evidence: tells.md section 9: "A non-native writer's formal style. Do not push it toward a template." SKILL.md Edit: "For a writer whose first language is not English, fix the grammar but do not make the phrasing sound native." tells.md section 8: "in one study they flagged 61% of essays by non-native English writers". Supported by DEVLOG 24 (learner essays).

items.rule: Preserve hard-to-fabricate specifics (dates, amounts, paths, names, measured numbers).
items.v14_evidence: SKILL.md hard rule 2: "When editing, every claim, hedge and number survives unless the user agrees to cut it." tells.md section 10: "Concrete names, dates, numbers and objects".

items.rule: Preserve mixed/unresolved feelings, admitted uncertainty, stated bias.
items.v14_evidence: SKILL.md hard rule 4: "leave strong sentences alone, including the writer's odd word choices, asides and mixed feelings." Hard rule 2: hedges survive. tells.md section 10: "mixed feelings and unresolved questions". Supported by DEVLOG 23 (v10 to v10.1).

items.rule: Preserve lived, sensory, first-person detail.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md section 10: "Concrete names, dates, numbers and objects; small true anecdotes". examples.md #3 keeps the ammonia-and-bleach detail as "the best thing here".

items.rule: Preserve era-bound or in-group voice: slang, references, jokes.
items.v14_evidence: SKILL.md Edit: "Keep everything else: their sentences and their order, vocabulary, repetitions, paragraphing, contractions, humor and punctuation habits." messages.md rule 7: "the team's own name and its in-jokes if the user gave them." Hard rule 3 bans only adding slang.

items.rule: Preserve deliberate imperfection: fragments, tangents, self-corrections, abrupt endings.
items.v14_evidence: Partly covered. Hard rule 4 keeps "asides and mixed feelings", and tells.md section 10 keeps "parenthetical asides" and "endings that stop on a specific point". But Edit also says "Cut clear AI tells if the text has them", and v14 lists fragment stacks (S9) and staged self-correction (S12) as tells, so it could cut a human writer's own fragments. One sentence saying the writer's own fragments, tangents and abrupt endings are voice would close the gap. DEVLOG 21 cue coding: "Uneven, digressions" was cited as a real-student sign in 51% of ratings of real essays.

items.rule: Do not modernize text written before late 2022.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md section 9: "Quotations, titles, names, and text written before late 2022."

items.rule: Restraint: over-editing launders a real voice; living text often needs no edit.
items.v14_evidence: SKILL.md hard rule 4: "Minimum effective edit on human-written text. Fix what is broken... If a passage is already clean, say so and return it unchanged." tells.md section 8: "Erasing the writer's voice by polishing everything to the same smooth surface." Strongly supported by DEVLOG 24.

items.rule: Ruthless-editor persona: don't just delete bad patterns, replace them with something lively.
items.v14_evidence: Breaks hard rule 1 ("A made-up specific is worse than the vague sentence it replaced") and hard rule 4 (minimum effective edit). "Replace with something that has a pulse" is what produces the invented specifics in nearly every humanizer example. DEVLOG 21: v8c's "attempted images"/"scenes" rules raised unsupported claims from 0.12 to 0.58 per essay and moved p(real) by -1.7.

items.rule: North star: resist regression to the mean; write weird, specific and inconsistent.
items.v14_evidence: The diagnosis is already in v14 (SKILL.md: "A language model picks the choice that fits the widest range of readers"). The prescription goes against our data. DEVLOG 23 short answers: judges caught model answers by over-crafting (quirky labels, comic asides, stacked figures), and "admitted students wrote plainer, more committed answers that judges rated lower as writing but never doubted". DEVLOG 21: v8c's "tries hard" rules brought invented details back.

items.rule: Text must reveal a specific mind with a stake; not done until a reader can picture a specific writer.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md C1: "Portability (strong). A sentence that could move unchanged into another person's essay ... says nothing." personal-essay.md section 1: "Admissions officers read an essay to meet a specific 17-year-old". SKILL.md step 4: arc and reflection check. v14 deliberately does not make this a gate for every genre (research.md wants the field's register), and when material is thin the gate can only be met by asking (v14) or inventing.

items.rule: No fabrication: may sharpen/cut/restructure, never invent facts, names, dates, numbers, quotes.
items.v14_evidence: SKILL.md hard rule 1: "use no fact, name, number, date, quote, source, anecdote, feeling or memory that they or their source did not provide." The humanizer's own examples break this rule repeatedly.

items.rule: When a needed concrete detail is missing, flag the gap or ask instead of inventing.
items.v14_evidence: SKILL.md hard rule 1: "If a sentence needs a detail you lack, ask, or write `[ask: what did your dad actually say?]`, or write a plainer sentence."

items.rule: If no text/file given, prompt to paste text or pass --file.
items.v14_evidence: CLI invocation detail. v14 Write mode already asks for missing material.

items.rule: Three modes: detect, rewrite (default, full transform), edit.
items.v14_evidence: v14 has Detect, Edit and Rebuild, but sends a user's text to Edit by default ("If the user's text is their own draft, use Edit"; Rebuild only if "the user says an AI wrote it... if you only suspect it, use Edit"). Full rewrite as the default is the condition DEVLOG 24 measured: plain "improve it" changed 73-93% of words and only 0-30% of texts were judged the writer's own, against 91-100% for minimum edits on abstracts and appeals. It also breaks hard rule 4.

items.rule: Without --voice, infer the voice from the input's register.
items.v14_evidence: SKILL.md Edit keeps the writer's "vocabulary, repetitions, paragraphing, contractions, humor and punctuation habits"; "If the user also gave a writing sample, it overrides the default style rules here, including the dash rule." In Write and Rebuild, v14 sets register from the genre notes, not from the input. Inferring register from an AI draft would copy the AI register.

items.rule: Auto-load humanizer-context.md (brand samples, banned phrases, preferred terms) as extra voice guidance.
items.v14_evidence: v14 honours a sample given in the conversation ("If the user also gave a writing sample, it overrides the default style rules here") and project rules ("When a project has its own writing rules ... follow them too"), but has no standing per-user voice file. Catalog O4/O5 name the writer's own samples as the fix for register mismatch and dash rate. Compatible if the file is the user's own, read as style data, and its facts count as user-supplied. Untested.

items.rule: --aggressive: heavier rewrite, shorter sentences, more personality, kill all hedging.
items.v14_evidence: Breaks hard rule 2: "every claim, hedge and number survives unless the user agrees to cut it. Never make a claim stronger than its evidence." tells.md section 8 lists "Stripping every hedge" as an over-correction. Shorter sentences also go against DEVLOG 21/22/23: real texts average 15 to 22 words per sentence, model texts 10 to 13.

items.rule: --purpose essay: no contractions, formal headings, structured arguments.
items.v14_evidence: DEVLOG 21: the v8 candidate's stiff, no-contraction register lost quality and its gain did not replicate (-0.2); v8b restored ordinary contractions. DEVLOG 24 regression check: "a personal statement with no contractions read like a form." On headings, tells.md section 7: "headings only where a reader navigates."

items.rule: --purpose email: greetings and sign-off allowed, no Markdown.
items.v14_evidence: messages.md rule 7: "A greeting is optional". SKILL.md genre notes: "sign off plainly". tells.md section 7: "Markdown residue (`**`, `##`) in text pasted into Word or a form. Remove."

items.rule: --purpose marketing: short paragraphs, concrete benefits, one CTA at the end.
items.v14_evidence: Product marketing is not a v14 genre. The nearest, appeals, already has messages.md rule 2 ("Put the ask at the end, or wherever it lands naturally") and rule 4 ("Keep the money concrete when the facts give it"). Benefits must come from the user's facts (hard rule 1). Untested.

items.rule: --purpose technical: preserve code, precise jargon, numbers over adjectives.
items.v14_evidence: research.md rule 7: "Technical terms stay technical and unexplained unless the notes define them". Rule 4: "Report results as numbers against a comparison." SKILL.md: "Skip it for code". tells.md T2: "the observable fact that earned the rating."

items.rule: --ignore-code/--ignore-quotes: mask code and block quotes, restore verbatim.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md section 9: "Quotations, titles, names..." are not acted on. SKILL.md: "Skip it for code". The masking itself is mechanics.

items.rule: Significance inflation ('stands as', 'testament', 'pivotal moment'): state what the thing is or does.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md T1: "Significance inflation. 'marked a pivotal moment', 'a testament to', 'reflects a broader shift'... Fix: keep the fact, drop the verdict."

items.rule: Notability name-dropping: replace outlet lists with one source and what it said, or cut.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md C6 covers unnamed sources ("Experts say") but not lists of named outlets used as proof. Safe only if the outlets the user gave are kept, or what one reported is stated where the source shows it, otherwise `[ask: ...]`. The humanizer's own example invents the year, the interview and the claim. Rare in our genres.

items.rule: Superficial -ing clauses: delete or promote to a sourced sentence.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md S4: "'-ing' tails (strong). A clause tacked on to interpret the fact... Fix: cut the tail". Catalog S3: measured at 2-5x the human rate (Reinhart).

items.rule: Promotional adjectives (nestled, vibrant, seamless, world-class): say what specifically makes it notable.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md T2: "Rating adjectives instead of description... Fix: the observable fact that earned the rating." tells.md section 6 lists vibrant, seamless, groundbreaking, transformative. The specific must come from the source (the humanizer's example invents a market and a church).

items.rule: Vague attributions: name the source or delete the claim.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md C6: "'Experts say', 'Studies show', 'Critics argue'. Fix: name the source and what it said, or cut the claim. Never invent a source."

items.rule: 'Despite challenges... continues to thrive' sections: state specific problems with data, or cut.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md T6: "'While X offers benefits, it also presents challenges.' Fix: take the position the evidence supports". S7 covers upbeat send-offs. The specifics must come from the source (C2: "never invent one").

items.rule: AI vocabulary by tier list: cut or use plain words.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md section 6: "Vocabulary (last pass; rewrite the sentence, never just swap the word)", with current-model and classic lists. Low intrinsic value: DEVLOG 1.2 ("Banning words backfires"); DEVLOG 21: the word-list condition was no more human than plain (+1.9 [-2.2, +6.0] held out).

items.rule: Copula avoidance: use is/are/has instead of serves as/boasts/features.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md section 6: "Plain-verb swaps that are always fine: serves as → is; boasts → has". SKILL.md step 2: "Use plain verbs (is, has, used, tried)."

items.rule: Negative parallelisms: state the point directly.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md S1 (strong): "Test: does anyone in this context actually believe X, and does rejecting X add information? If not, state Y." v14 acts on one unlicensed sighting; the humanizer waits for two.

items.rule: Rule of three: use the natural count.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md S8: "Fix: keep the items that are distinct and true. Vary list lengths." SKILL.md Rhythm row: "keep list items that are distinct (often two, sometimes four)". The humanizer's example adds event content.

items.rule: Synonym cycling: pick one term and repeat it.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md R4: "Elegant variation... Fix: repeat the precise term."

items.rule: False ranges ('from X to Y' not on a real spectrum): name the actual items.
items.v14_evidence: Not in v14 or our catalog. Compatible if the fix names only items already in the text.

items.rule: Em dash zero tolerance: replace every U+2014 with commas, colons or hyphens.
items.v14_evidence: v14 R6 avoids dashes in text it writes, but "A user's own drafts or style rules override this". DEVLOG 22: the dash-to-colon swap became a tell ("The skill's Format rule ('commas, colons or parentheses instead of dashes') pushes toward the semicolon and colon tell"). DEVLOG 21: admitted essays use 0.17 dashes per 100 words against 0 in every model version. DEVLOG 24: dashes separate real essays from model ones at AUC 0.998. Zero dashes is the model signature.

items.rule: Formatting overuse (bold everywhere, emoji, skipped heading levels, tables): bold once per section.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md section 7: "Bold run-in labels... Turn into prose", "Emoji in anything formal. Remove", Title Case and heading frequency, "Bullets where an argument belongs". Minor gaps: scattered emphasis bold, skipped heading levels, tables (see P42).

items.rule: Structured-list syndrome ('**Bold Header:** description'): write paragraphs.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md section 7: "Bullets where an argument belongs. Write paragraphs"; "Bold run-in labels ('**Transparency:** Transparency is…'). Turn into prose."

items.rule: Title Case headings: use sentence case.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md section 7: "Title Case Headings ... Use sentence case".

items.rule: Curly quotes and rigid Oxford comma as model fingerprints: match the author's typography.
items.v14_evidence: SKILL.md Edit keeps the writer's "punctuation habits". tells.md section 9 treats curly quotes as one weak tell. tells.md section 7 matches the destination for Markdown. The "ChatGPT curly / Claude straight" framing is a fingerprint scrub with no benefit to the reader; SKILL.md Integrity: "It is not a way to hide AI use." DEVLOG 21: typography differences were an artifact of the four-way design and were normalized away.

items.rule: Formal-register overuse ('it should be noted that'): drop to the register context calls for.
items.v14_evidence: SKILL.md: "One register for everything. The same polished, noun-heavy voice in a lab report and a personal story." tells.md section 6: "it's important to note", "it's worth noting". A blanket push to plain register would be wrong for our genres: DEVLOG 21 found admitted essays use more abstract nouns (2.9 per 100 words against 1.0-1.2 in model versions), and DEVLOG 23 found real abstracts denser and more passive.

items.rule: Chatbot artifacts ('I hope this helps', 'Certainly!'): delete.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md T8: "Chatbot residue. 'Great question', 'I hope this helps', 'Let me know if…', 'Certainly!'. Delete."

items.rule: Knowledge-cutoff disclaimers: state the fact or cut the hedge.
items.v14_evidence: v14 T8 lists chatbot residue but not cutoff disclaimers. Catalog P9 has the safer fix: "say exactly what is missing". Importing it means deleting the chatbot wording and keeping the uncertainty. The humanizer's literal fix is unsafe: "state the fact" without the fact breaks hard rule 1, and cutting a real hedge breaks hard rule 2 ("Never make a claim stronger than its evidence").

items.rule: Sycophantic tone: answer without flattery.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md T8 ("Great question") and T9: "Sycophantic feedback... praise only specific lines that work." SKILL.md Detect: "praise only specific things that work."

items.rule: Filler phrases ('in order to', 'due to the fact that'): delete or shorten.
items.v14_evidence: Not a v14 tell. Catalog section 12 lists "Isolated wordy constructions humans use ('in order to', 'the fact that')" as signs of human writing (WP). On a user's own text, cutting them is not fixing what is broken (hard rule 4). Compatible only in text Claude writes, and not worth importing.

items.rule: Stacked hedges: commit, or state the one real uncertainty.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md T5: "Hedge stacks... Fix: one hedge, on the uncertain part. Keep hedges that carry real uncertainty". Supported by DEVLOG 23: hedges were cited in 31-38% of model-abstract ratings against 6% of real ones.

items.rule: Generic positive conclusions: end on a specific fact or open question.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md S7: "Upbeat send-offs... Fix: state the actual next step or the limit." An open question as the default ending is contradicted by DEVLOG 21: v7's "honest open question" advice produced shrug endings, while admitted essays end committed. v14 allows one only "when the student really is unsure".

items.rule: Hallucination markers (suspicious numbers, nonexistent sources): verify or cut.
items.v14_evidence: SKILL.md step 4: "Fact diff: list every name, number, date, quote and claim in the output and confirm each comes from the user or the source." Rebuild: "First check each of its facts, quotes and claims against the user's material".

items.rule: Perfect prose alternating with basic errors suggests partial edit: hold one quality level.
items.v14_evidence: SKILL.md Edit: "Fix outright errors (spelling, grammar, agreement, articles, punctuation)" everywhere, so the error level is uniform. Detect does not infer partial AI editing ("Do not guess whether a human or a model wrote it"). Raising human-written parts to polish would break hard rule 4.

items.rule: Question-format section titles: use statement headings in long-form.
items.v14_evidence: Not in v14 or the catalog. Fine in long-form text Claude writes. On a user's own report it belongs in the suggestions list (hard rule 4).

items.rule: Markdown bleeding: strip where it won't render.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md section 7: "Markdown residue (`**`, `##`) in text pasted into Word or a form. Remove."

items.rule: 'In this article we will explore' openings: start with the content.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md S3: "'In this essay I will explore'... Fix: start with the claim." SKILL.md step 2: "Start with the first real claim, scene or result."

items.rule: Uniform sentence length: mix short and long.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md R1: "Uniform sentence length (strong in aggregate)... Fix: vary length where the meaning changes pace... Never chop at random."

items.rule: Noun-phrase elegant variation: pick the clearest term and repeat it.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md R4: "Renaming the same thing each time (Unilever, the firm, the conglomerate, the multinational)... Fix: repeat the precise term."

items.rule: Chat framing in published text ('let me walk you through'): delete.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md S3: "'Here's the thing', 'Let's break this down'... Fix: start with the claim." T8: "Let me know if…". Delete.

items.rule: Placeholder/mad-libs text ([Your Name]): fill in or delete.
items.v14_evidence: Flagging leftover template placeholders in user text is useful. Fill them only from the user's material (hard rule 1). Never delete v14's own `[ask: ...]` brackets, which are its designed output (hard rule 1: "write `[ask: ...]`").

items.rule: Delete chatbot citation markup (citeturn0search0, oaicite, [cite: 1]...), add a real reference if it mattered.
items.v14_evidence: Not in v14. These tokens are paste junk readers can see, like the Markdown residue tells.md section 7 already removes. Limits: add a reference only if the user supplies it, otherwise use research.md's `[cite: source for X]` ("Never invent a citation"). Caution: Gemini's "[cite: 1]" looks like v14's own `[cite: ...]` placeholder, so a naive strip would delete v14's brackets. This is cleanup, not watermark removal, and it does not change disclosure duties (SKILL.md Integrity).

items.rule: Strip AI-tool UTM parameters (utm_source=chatgpt.com, referrer=grok.com) from URLs.
items.v14_evidence: Breaks hard rule 3 ("No tricks... the point of this skill is good writing") and SKILL.md Integrity: "This skill makes writing better for its reader. It is not a way to hide AI use." The parameter is invisible in a rendered link; its only effect is to show the link came from an AI tool, so stripping it serves concealment, not the reader. General link cleanup the user asks for is ordinary hygiene, not writing.

items.rule: Sudden style/register or spelling shifts: hold one register; rewrite AI sections to match the author.
items.v14_evidence: v14 has Rebuild and lets a writing sample override style rules, but does not tell it to look for register or US/UK spelling switches inside one document. Consistent spelling is an outright-error fix. Rewriting AI sections into the author's voice is fine for non-graded prose. For college essays and graded work it would be ghostwriting (hard rule 5: coach instead). The humanizer's example invents content.

items.rule: Overattribution ('featured in A, B and other outlets'): pick one source and what it reported.
items.v14_evidence: Same as P02: only from what the source shows, else `[ask: ...]`. The humanizer's example invents "Wired profiled her 2024 research".

items.rule: Paragraph-reshuffling immunity: make each paragraph depend on the last; merge interchangeable mini-theses.
items.v14_evidence: "Make each paragraph depend on the last" pushes toward the engineered structure our judges cite most. DEVLOG 21 cue coding: tidy, engineered structure was cited as AI in 75-86% of ratings of every model version. v8b removed connective sentences and callbacks: +7.5 p(real) held out, and unsupported claims fell from 1.50 to 0.12. DEVLOG 23 r1: stitched cause-and-effect links were cited in abstracts. Admitted essays are loose (personal-essay.md: "a list of what the student learned, a year-by-year account, a side detail"). Only the argument-genre version is supported (DEVLOG 13: one organizing idea), and v14 has it ("Pick a position and hold it"; Rebuild "your own organizing idea").

items.rule: 'Whether you...' recaps and 'In summary/Overall' enders: cut, end on the strongest point.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md S6: "Summary closers (strong at paragraph level)... 'In conclusion'; 'Ultimately,'... Fix: end on the last new point". research.md rule 8 cuts "Overall". Not absolute: DEVLOG 23 found admitted short answers "often end on a plain summary line", and short-answers.md keeps that.

items.rule: Symbolic gloss ('represents', 'symbolizes', 'embodies'): state the fact, let the reader interpret.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md C4: "Redundant exposition. Telling the reader what the example just showed... Fix: delete; let the example work." personal-essay.md section 5: "Comment on meaning once... let scenes, quotes and contrasts stand without a sentence that explains them." Supported by DEVLOG 21 (v8b).

items.rule: Infomercial hooks ('The catch?', 'Here's the thing.'): delete.
items.v14_evidence: tells.md S3: "'Here's the thing'... 'The answer? Simple.' Fix: start with the claim."

items.rule: Erratic inline bolding: strip except glossary terms and UI labels.
items.v14_evidence: v14 tells.md section 7 covers bold run-in labels only. Catalog F3 has the broader rule ("bold scattered for emphasis on every key term... use bold rarely"). Fine in text Claude writes; on a user's own text it goes beyond minimum edit.

items.rule: Treadmill effect ('In other words', 'Put simply'): delete sentences that add nothing new.
