items.rule: (Flagged content) 'designed for long-term [X]': cut 'designed for' and state the property.
items.v14_evidence: Breaks hard rule 2 ('Never make a claim stronger than its evidence'): a stated design intent becomes an asserted property.

items.rule: (Flagged content) 'testament to → shows, proves, demonstrates' and 'hit differently → affects [me/us] differently'.
items.v14_evidence: 'proves' raises certainty (hard rule 2); '[me/us]' can insert a first-person speaker the input lacked (hard rule 1).

items.rule: (Flagged content) Lingering-attention Fix example: 'The line I keep coming back to: agents are teenagers' becomes 'Agents are teenagers.'
items.v14_evidence: Hard rule 2: a quoted line becomes the writer's own assertion (attribution and stance shift).

items.rule: (Flagged content) Scenario-opener Fix example: 'Imagine a world where every deploy is instant' becomes 'Every deploy would be instant.'
items.v14_evidence: Hard rule 2 (minor): an invitation to imagine becomes the writer's own conditional claim.

items.rule: (Flagged content, README rows not loaded by the skill) Rows 6, 22, 27, 38, 40, 42, 43, 49 ask for specifics with no source condition ('rewrite each item as a full claim with a verb and a number', 'X may exceed Y by 2027'); row 53's after adds a review judgment ('this looks right to me') and an em dash.
items.v14_evidence: Hard rule 1 (invented specifics) and hard rule 2 (row 53 adds a position the writer did not take). Do not copy README examples.

items.rule: (Flagged content, README row 34, not loaded) 'Mix short/long, fragments, questions'.
items.v14_evidence: DEVLOG 21 cue coding: 'Short punchy beats' were read as AI in 42% (plain) and 57% (word list) of ratings and never for real essays; DEVLOG 1.1: humanizer rewrites added aphoristic closers (38 to 61). tells.md sec 8 already forbids 'Chopping sentences into fragments for "burstiness"'.

checks.reason: Already covered as a class. tells.md S3: "Run-ups and signposts. 'Here's the thing', 'Let's break this down' ... Fix: start with the claim." The SKILL.md Staging row and step 4 also apply: "Does any sentence only exist to sound good?" Section 6 already lists "the real question". The extra openers are more instances of the same class. The catalog grades the class M but the specific openers only C (P2). Two parts would hurt. First, stop-slop says to delete every instance, while v14 acts on unmarked entries only in aggregate and makes minimum edits to human text. Second, 'It turns out' carries meaning (a finding that went against expectation), so deleting it breaks hard rule 2. Stop-slop's own 'after' texts for these deletions come out as staccato fragments ('Technology is manageable. People aren't.'), which S9 and S11 call a tell. In our runs none of 'It turns out', 'The truth is' or 'The reality is' appears in about 17k words of plain-model text, so there is no sign they are current-model habits in our genres. The section 24 ablation showed that removing tells.md entirely did not lower human-likeness, so more list entries are unlikely to help, and Antislop warns that listing phrases can backfire. DEVLOG 1.1 already took what was worth taking from this list.

This rule would hurt. 'Here's the thing' is already in S3. Cutting any 'here's what/this/that' conflicts with v14's own punctuation rule. R5 says to "keep a colon only before a list, a quote or a link", and the SKILL.md Format row says "a colon only before a list, quote or link". So 'Here's the plan for Saturday:' followed by a list is allowed. messages.md wants the news and the request in the first two lines of an action message, and that is exactly where people write 'Here's what we need'. The blog genre note asks for "a real opening (what happened, what you found)", and 'Here's what happened' is a normal human opener. No catalog frequency evidence supports it (P2, grade C). In our counts 'Here's/Here is' appears 0.4 times per 10k words in learner essays and 1.2 in plain-model text, but the model figure is only 2 hits, which is not meaningful.

Already covered. 'This matters because' and 'Here's why that matters' fall under tells.md S2 (strong): "Importance flags ... 'This matters because', 'Why this matters:' ... Fix: give the consequence". 'Let that sink in.', 'Full stop.' and 'Period.' are one-line punchlines that flag importance. S9 covers them ("Fragment stacks and one-line punchlines ... A one-sentence paragraph after every section"), as do S11 kicker endings and the step-4 over-correction check. The catalog files 'Let that sink in' under S6 with grade C only. 'Make no mistake' has no evidence at all: zero hits in the learner essays and in our plain-model texts. Naming more instances of classes v14 already acts on adds nothing measurable (section 24 ablation).

This rule would hurt. A fixed swap table contradicts v14's method. tells.md section 6 is headed "rewrite the sentence, never just swap the word", the SKILL.md Words row says "do not just swap the word", and section 8 lists thesaurus swaps as an over-correction. Some of its replacements are themselves tells: 'significant' outside a statistical test is flagged (section 9 allows it only "with a test"; catalog RP2), and 'embrace' is stock. As detection entries only, 'circle back', 'deep dive', 'on the same page', 'double down', 'moving forward' and 'take a step back' are office jargon people wrote long before 2022. We have no evidence that models use them more. Flagging them would mark human business writing as AI, against section 9's guard for "text written before late 2022". The two jargon words with evidence, 'landscape' and 'navigate', are already in section 6, and hype such as 'game-changing' falls under T1 and the classic list ('groundbreaking', 'transformative').

This rule would hurt. DEVLOG 1.1 rejected stop-slop's adverb ban by name as an over-correction ("no adverbs"). On pre-2022 learner essays (ELLIPSE, 1.7M words), 'just' appears 26.3 times and 'really' 15.8 times per 10k words, against 16.3 and 4.7 in plain-model text. These are human habits, more common in human text than in plain model text. Deleting them on a user's draft breaks hard rule 4 and tells.md section 10, which keeps casual qualifiers in informal writing. 'just' and 'simply' often mean 'only' or 'recently', and 'inevitably' asserts necessity, so cutting them breaks hard rule 2. 'fundamentally', 'inherently', 'inevitably', 'interestingly' and 'crucially' never appear in our plain-model texts, so there is no sign of a current habit. The parts with evidence are already in v14: T3 (genuinely, truly, deeply, honestly), the classic list ('crucial'; 'Notably' opening several sentences) and the speech-filler rules for text written from notes. In EB3 the stop-slop package, which contains this rule, changed 90% of the words in learner essays. It added 3.98 statements per text, scored 3.65 out of 10 on voice kept, and rated below plain on p(the writer's own): -3.9, interval -6.0 to -2.1.

Covered where evidence exists. tells.md section 6 already has "in today's fast-paced world", "it's worth noting" and "it's important to note". C7 (low density), the SKILL.md Content row ("padding the reader could infer") and step 4 handle filler in general. The new phrases look like human clichés, not model tells. Per 10k words in pre-2022 learner essays: 'When it comes to' 0.7, 'At the end of the day' 0.5, 'In a world where' 0.1. All three appear zero times in about 17k words of our plain-model text. Cutting them from a user's draft breaks the minimum-edit rule. 'At its core' is the only one with measured support (Graphite, catalog P3), and that support is described as declining. It also appears zero times in our outputs. One borderline entry does not justify taking the rule.

Partly covered, and the rest would hurt. In model-written text, R5 and the Format row already remove colon reveals such as 'Hint:', 'Plot twist:' and 'Spoiler:'. PE10's framing devices ('(I counted)') and short-answers.md's "comic asides" cover the class. 'You already know this, but' is S5 territory (arguing with no one). 'But that's another post' is a habit human bloggers really have. DEVLOG 15 found blog posts to be the skill's weak genre and said "the skill's audit may strip the looseness these genres want", so cutting more blog-register asides points the wrong way. The catalog has no evidence for any of these.

No evidence, and it conflicts with v14. 'creeps in' is an ordinary verb phrase, not a sincerity marker. 'I promise' is a real writer's voice in casual messages, and tells.md section 10 keeps informal-register signals ("casual qualifiers", "an occasional exclamation in informal writing"). The catalog grades even 'honestly' U as a measured tell (V4). None of these phrases appears in the learner essays or our model texts. Edit mode would leave them alone, and Write mode never produced them, so the rule changes nothing.

Covered where it is a tell, harmful where it is not. The staged version is a temporal form of corrective framing, and S1's test already applies: "does anyone in this context actually believe X, and does rejecting X add information? If not, state Y." The catalog's S1 list includes 'no longer X. It is Y.' PE2 covers tidy transformation arcs in essays. 'Stopped being X and started being Y' is also the literal way to report a real change, so a blanket 'avoid' risks hard rule 2. In our counts 'stop(s/ped) being' appears 0.1 times per 10k words for learners and 0.6 for plain model (one hit in 17k words). That is no evidence.

This rule conflicts with v14 genre rules built from data. messages.md (32 real appeals) lets an appeal open on "the question that made the writer run ... 'Did you know...?'". The SKILL.md explanations note says to "start from a question a reader actually has". S3 already covers staged rhetorical setups. Pre-2022 learner essays use 'What if' 0.7 times per 10k words, and our plain-model texts never do. The catalog has no evidence for it.

Already in the S3 class ("Run-ups and signposts ... Fix: start with the claim"), and R5 removes the colon in model-written text. 'Think about it' appears 0.7 times per 10k words in pre-2022 learner essays and zero times in our plain-model texts. It is a human habit rather than a model one, and Edit mode should keep it in a writer's draft. The catalog has no evidence.

This rule would remove ordinary narrative English. 'By the time X, I was Y' is a plain time clause, and personal-essay.md notes that admitted essays often tell their stories in order. Rates are about the same in human and model text: 0.9 per 10k words in learner essays, 1.2 in plain model (two hits). No catalog or DEVLOG evidence supports it. Banning it would push writers toward less natural sentences, the opposite of the skill's aim.

This rule would hurt. Its fix, "Name the human" or else use 'you', runs into hard rule 1 when the source names no actor, and 'you' is wrong in research register. It also collides with research.md, where "'Table 2 shows' is a convention, not a tell", passive voice is normal in methods, and 'the data show' is standard. Metonymy such as 'the market rewards' or 'the school decided' is ordinary English. Stop-slop's companion rules ("No passive constructions", "Every sentence needs a human subject") were rejected in DEVLOG 1.1 as damaging academic prose. The cases that are real tells are figurative personification, which T4 (mannered prose) already covers, and repeated generic openers, which R3 covers. The catalog has no frequency evidence.

This is the strongest candidate, but there is not enough evidence yet. Our quick count does show a model excess. Pseudo-cleft statements of the form 'What X is/was Y' (questions excluded) appear 2.8 to 5.0 times per 10k words in plain-model texts from phases 2 and 3, and 5.5 in skill v4/v6 texts, against 0.8 in 1.7M words of learner essays. Examples: 'What hit us was outflow...', 'What I told nobody is that...'. But the model sample is tiny (7 plain hits in 17k words). It is confounded by genre (learner essays against personal statements and literary analyses). It has no admitted-essay or ISEF comparison, and v14 outputs were not counted. Where the pattern works as a reveal, v14 already covers it: personal-essay.md bans signposts such as "What I didn't expect" and "The strange part was", and PE11 and S3 cover the rest. In literary analysis or argument, pseudo-clefts are a normal human way to place emphasis. Stop-slop's preferred fix ('name the specific constraint') invites adding content the source lacks (hard rule 1). Recommendation: count pseudo-clefts in the private admitted-essay and ISEF corpora against v14 outputs before writing any rule.

Already handled by v14's register rules, and the data say they work. messages.md rule 8 says "Leave the notes' spoken tics behind", personal-essay.md says to "Drop speech filler", and SKILL.md lists forced casualness as an over-correction. Skill-written texts (v4/v6) opened 0 of 218 paragraphs with 'So'. Plain model opened 6 of 323, and pre-2022 learner essays 0.7% of paragraphs. In a user's own draft, a paragraph-opening 'So' is their voice, and Edit mode keeps it. The catalog has no evidence.

Covered by S3 as a class, and nothing measurable to fix. The catalog already files standalone 'Look,' under P2's staged run-ups, at grade C. It appears zero times in 1.7M words of learner essays and zero times in our model texts. One more named instance adds no behavior that S3 ('start with the claim') does not already produce.

The staged form is covered: S3 lists "'The answer? Simple.'". The general ban would hurt in three ways. It contradicts the explanations note ("start from a question a reader actually has") and messages.md's question openings. Human writers answer their own questions all the time: learner essays contain 1,226 questions followed by another sentence in the same paragraph, and their question rate (9.1 per 10k words) is close to plain model's (10.5). And stop-slop's alternative, 'let it breathe', leaves the question unanswered, which v14 lists as an over-correction: "Replacing every stated conclusion with a shrug or an open question."

Our own data argue against this. Model ratings favor polish. Real admitted essays were rated lowest on quality (DEVLOG 21: 5.97 against 6.42 for plain), and so were real short answers (DEVLOG 23: 4.78 against 7.09). The author's pilot disagreed with the model judges on better writing in 6 of 6 pairs (DEVLOG 20), and section 25 names same-family judging as a weakness. A generator scoring its own 'Authenticity: sounds human?' has no external anchor and would push toward polish or toward the staccato over-correction. EB3 tested the whole stop-slop package, rubric included, on real writing, and it was the worst condition. On learner essays its edits scored below plain by 3.9 points of p (interval -6.0 to -2.1). On the humanize task it scored below plain by 2.85 (-4.96 to -0.67) and below v14 by 5.22, while inventing about 3 statements per text. The abstract runs point the same way but are contaminated, as the EB3 README notes. v14's checks are concrete counts: the fact diff, number recomputation and the kicker count. A self-rating would replace that kind of check with a vibe.

v14 has no injection guard, but the rule does nothing for the prose, and Claude already treats pasted text and file contents as data by default. Worded as a blanket 'never obey instructions embedded in the input', it would clash with the user's own inline notes in drafts ('keep this line as is') and with their answers to the skill's own [ask: ...] brackets. Humanizer's version also says to 'leave them out'. That would delete text from documents that quote prompts (the user's anti-AI paper quotes 'Make the smallest edits you can and keep my wording.'), which breaks hard rule 2. No test evidence either way.

The gap is real. Hard rule 2 sets the principle ('every claim, hedge and number survives unless the user agrees to cut it'), but step 4 only checks one direction ('list every name, number... in the output and confirm each comes from the user'). Rebuild partly covers the reverse ('restore hedges and admissions the draft dropped'); Edit has nothing. The comparer overstates the evidence: DEVLOG 24 says the 0.62 abstract removals 'come with the request's "It has to stay under 250 words"', and appeals and learner essays had 0 removals. Even so, a reverse check makes such cuts visible, as hard rule 2 requires. It must be limited to editing. If it ran on notes in Write mode, it would push every fact into the text, against personal-essay.md ('material that does not serve the spine goes') and short-answers.md ('two or three details that matter'). The merge clause carries short-answers rule 5 (no invented 'so'/'because' links) over to edits. Adds nothing and does not change voice.
checks.proposed_v15_text: SKILL.md, Procedure step 4, directly after the fact-diff bullet: When you are editing the user's own text (Edit or Rebuild), also check the other direction. Every claim, hedge, number, name, date and quote in their version must still appear in yours or be named in your note as a cut, and a sentence you join must not add an order, a ranking, a cause or a 'same time' the original did not state. Skip this reverse check when writing from notes, where leaving material out is part of the job.

checks.reason: v14 already has the read-through and the new-tell check in step 4 ('Read it as the target reader. Does any sentence only exist to sound good?'; 'Did the rewrite create new tells?' plus the kicker count). Humanizer's survivor sweep targets §8 dashes and §6 triads. On human text, v14's Edit mode keeps 'punctuation habits', and our data show dashes are a human signal: in DEVLOG 21, real essays used 0.17 dashes per 100 words and every model version used 0; in DEVLOG 24, dashes were the strongest single feature separating real essays from model ones (AUC 0.998). A second sweep would push human text toward model text, against hard rule 4 and the rule to act on weak tells only 'when several cluster'.

v14 only says a sample 'overrides the default style rules here, including the dash rule', and only in Edit. Write has no sample instruction, and nothing says what to match. Our data back matching measurable habits. In DEVLOG 22, punctuating like the register gave +11.7 p(human) held out. In DEVLOG 24, punctuation and sentence length alone separate real essays from model ones (AUC 0.997), and dashes were the top feature, which humans use and models do not. Catalog O4 ('use the student's own voice samples when available') and O5 ('keep their rate') say the same. Limits needed for the hard rules: the sample must be the user's own writing (an AI-polished 'sample' would bring tells back); match habits, not exact phrases, facts or errors (hard rules 1 and 3); no effect in Coach, where the student writes.
checks.proposed_v15_text: SKILL.md, Modes, at the end of both Write and Edit (replacing Edit's last sentence): If the user gives a sample of their own writing, read it before drafting and match the habits you can count in it: sentence length and spread, contractions, dashes, colons and semicolons, how sentences open and connect, and how formal the vocabulary is. These override the default style rules, but do not copy the sample's facts, exact phrases or errors into the new text, and in Coach mode the sample changes nothing because the student still writes.

checks.reason: v14 contradicts itself here. Edit says 'Cut clear AI tells' and fix outright 'spelling... punctuation' errors, and the Rhythm row lists 'fragment stacks ('No plan. No data. No excuse.')' as a tell. So a user's 'Worst. Service. Ever.' or a lowercase chat message could be 'fixed', even though Edit also says to keep 'punctuation habits' and messages.md says 'In the user's own text, leave their punctuation'. Catalog section 13 calls mixed registers an ineffective indicator. Section 10 keeps casual qualifiers and exclamations in informal writing but says nothing about lowercase, abbreviations or fragments. The carve-out must cover only the user's own text. Adding these features to text the model writes is forced casualness (hard rule 3; over-corrections list; examples.md #9).
checks.proposed_v15_text: tells.md section 9 (When not to act), with a one-line pointer from Edit mode: In the user's own informal text (a chat message, a comment, a review, a casual post), lowercase, short forms like 'lmk', fragments and emphatic stops such as 'Worst. Service. Ever.' are part of the register, not errors or tells, so leave them and fix only what blocks the meaning. This protects what the user wrote; never add these features to text you write.

checks.reason: This is agent housekeeping, not a writing rule. In Claude Code the Edit tool refuses to change a file that has not been read and flags files that changed since the last read. The project's CLAUDE.md already requires reading the live report before proposing edits ('ALWAYS download and read the current version'). The skill is also uploaded to claude.ai, where there is no disk. It has no effect on the prose.

v14 says only 'Skip it for code, data tables and one-line chat answers' and says nothing about prose mixed with markup. That case is real here. The user's anti-AI paper is LaTeX (research/anti-ai-writing/paper/main.*), where '--' is the en dash in number ranges and citation keys and \ref labels must not change. CLAUDE.md routes all paper prose through this skill, while R6 and the Format row tell the model to remove dashes and colons. paper/design_decisions.md carries paths and commands such as '--company'. Step 5 also never says that Edit's list and number flags go in the reply, not into the file. This protects content only: nothing is invented and voice is unchanged.
checks.proposed_v15_text: SKILL.md, the opening scope paragraph and step 5 (Output): When prose sits in a file alongside code, commands, paths, URLs, YAML front matter, LaTeX markup, citation keys or data, edit only the prose and leave the rest exactly as it is, dashes and hyphens included. Write only the finished text into the file, and give Edit's list, any number flag and any note about cuts in your reply.

checks.reason: A process report with no effect on the prose. v14 step 5 deliberately limits output to 'only what the mode or the reference calls for... in a few lines'. Saying when part of a long file was not covered is already required by Claude's general honesty norms and CLAUDE.md's 'verify before asserting'.

'Return only the final text' breaks v14 rules that require notes after the text. Hard rule 2: 'If you cut a sentence because it is a tell..., say so after the text'. Step 4: if two numbers disagree, 'say so in one line after the text and ask'. research.md also requires an AI-use reminder. When the research-paper skill calls this one, those notes still matter to the user. PR and commit messages are outside v14's scope, and Claude Code has its own conventions for them.

Four of the five variants are already in tells.md S1 ('not just X but Y', 'X rather than Y', 'This isn't about X. It's about Y.') and section 6 ('rather than merely'). The clipped negative tail has only blader as a source in our catalog (grade C, no measurement). S1 is marked 'strong' (act on one sighting), so adding the tail would catch ordinary idioms in human text ('no questions asked', 'no exceptions'), against hard rule 4. S1's own test (does anyone believe X; does rejecting X add information) already applies when a tail really rejects a non-claim.

S1's test is already language-neutral: 'does anyone in this context actually believe X, and does rejecting X add information?'. Our only measurement in the user's second language points elsewhere. In DEVLOG 22 (192 rationales on Turkish appeals), judges caught model texts by semicolons and colons, the circumflex, an assembled plan, 'bence' and sentence shape, not by corrective framing. Peng's Mandarin data show humans use the construction too (33.3% of human uses also unneeded, against 52.8% for models). Spreading a one-sighting 'strong' tell to Turkish without Turkish evidence risks cutting human constructions in Edit. Unsure, so false.

The catalog has no measurement for ALL-CAPS emphasis (blader only). Current Claude rarely writes it, while people do in informal writing, so removing it takes out something human writers do. Period-separated words for drama are a fragment stack, already covered by S9 and the Rhythm row ('fragment stacks'). 'every single' is in T3.

Mostly covered. T4 handles the aphorism family ('trust is the currency of reporting', 'a mirror, not a window'; 'Fix: the literal statement'), and section 6 has 'the real question'. Of the rest, 'at its core' is declining (catalog P3), and 'fundamentally' has ordinary research uses ('fundamentally different methods') that would become false positives. Our evidence ranks vocabulary lists lowest (DEVLOG 1: word-list lift 0.9; DEVLOG 24 ablation: the tells catalog adds little). Humanizer's own §3 fixes add claims ('That mostly depends on whether the organization is ready to change its habits').

The carve-out is not needed in Edit. T3 is not marked strong, so by tells.md's own header a lone 'honestly' in user text is already left alone (section 9: 'One weak tell alone'; hard rule 4). The staged-question opener is covered by S3 ('The answer? Simple.'). Saying 'honestly' is fine inside casual sentences would also clash with personal-essay.md section 10 ('Drop speech filler (really, kind of, actually, basically, stuff, super, honestly) except inside quoted speech'). That rule rests on measured data (PE10 / DEVLOG 21: v7 used 'really' four times as often as admitted essays, and 'kind of' 12.1 per 10,000 words against 0).

S3 already covers run-ups and signposts in general ('Fix: start with the claim'). The form is named where we measured it, in personal essays (PE11 'signposts ("The strange part was")'; personal-essay.md section 10; DEVLOG 21). In general prose, 'The hard part is getting the data' names the thing and is ordinary human phrasing. No measurement supports it outside essays, and humanizer's fix example adds facts not in its 'before' text.

No catalog entry or measurement makes hyphen placement a tell. DEVLOG 21 lists 'wrong hyphens' among real students' errors that models do not make, so normalizing a human's hyphens moves the text toward model output. A real error is already fixed under Edit's outright-error rule.

The class is covered. T2 ('Rating adjectives instead of description... Fix: the observable fact') takes in breathtaking, stunning and renowned; T1 covers significance; section 6 has vibrant, groundbreaking, transformative, seamless and boast. Catalog V5 says Claude's hype words are declining across versions. 'nestled' and 'in the heart of' are Wikipedia-travel and older-GPT tells. In the user's genre where promotion might matter (appeals), DEVLOG 22 judges cited punctuation and plan, not promotional words, and our ablations show word lists add least. In a user's informal travel post, 'stunning' is ordinary human enthusiasm.

This targets Wikipedia biographies, which are not among the skill's genres. In text the user supplies (a bio, a cover letter, an activity list), the outlets are facts the writer chose. Cutting them breaks hard rule 2 and the minimum edit, and short-answers.md asks activity entries to show scale and level of recognition. Humanizer's own fix invents a '2024 New York Times interview'.

v14 never treats an unsourced claim as a tell, except vague attribution in C6 ('Experts say', 'Studies show'), and Edit forbids adding authority. Outside research the carve-out changes nothing. Inside research it contradicts research.md ('"Studies show" with no citation is not acceptable').

Low value and partly covered. Section 7 already handles bold run-in labels and Markdown residue in pasted text. The catalog's grade-A support (Russell, 'bolded lists') is about lists, which is the run-in case. The skill's tested genres (essays, appeals, abstracts, messages) rarely carry bold. In Edit, bold is the user's formatting (hard rule 4), and Rebuild rewrites the format anyway. Unsure of the benefit, so false.
Markdown-only formatting with grade-C support (catalog F5, WP only). None of the skill's tested genres uses section rules, and in Edit the layout is the user's choice. No measured benefit.

T4 mannered prose already applies wherever it appears, headings included. There is no measurement. Witty headings are a normal human choice in blogs and features, a genre where DEVLOG 15 found the skill already strips the looseness the genre wants ('The skill's audit may strip the looseness these genres want').

'as of [date]' is standard provenance in the user's own field. ESG reports date every figure, and research.md requires that 'Every number states what it was measured on', so flagging it would produce false positives in GreenBERT writing. Catalog P9 calls the disclaimer family 'mainly a GPT-6 tell; Claude drafts are less prone'. The guessing half is already covered by hard rule 1 and Rebuild's 'check each of its facts, quotes and claims against the user's material'. A topic-only Rebuild rewrites from step 1 anyway.

The usual forms are already strong tells in v14. Humanizer's own example, 'Speed matters.', and 'Data quality is important.' are S2 importance flags ('This matters because', 'is key to'). C7 covers the rest ('two sentences doing one job'; 'each sentence must add a fact, a reason or a step the reader lacks'), and so does research.md ('What goes is empty self-description'). In research writing, a short section opener tied to content is a convention v14 protects.

The one genre where this habit shows up in the user's work is research and project logs. There research.md requires provenance ('Every number states what it was measured on, the sample size, and whether it is in-sample'), and a caveat about unconfirmed figures is what its limitations rule asks for. Our data did not observe the habit in essays, appeals or messages. Humanizer's fix adds facts ('Two vendors publish nothing; call them').

v14 explicitly protects the research form (SKILL.md: 'Signposting ("Table 2 shows")... [is a convention], not [a tell]'; research.md: '"Table 2 shows" is a convention, not a tell'). Humanizer itself marks the pattern weak alone. Outside research it is rare in the skill's genres, so the value is negligible.

tells.md section 9 protects 'Quotations, titles, names, and text written before late 2022' but has no use/mention clause, though catalog section 13 does ('passages that discuss a word rather than use it'). This matters in this project. CLAUDE.md routes all paper prose through the skill, and the user's anti-AI paper, DEVLOG and LEDGER name 'delve', 'this matters' and 'It's not X, it's Y' as examples, often without quotation marks (in italics or LaTeX markup). Without the clause, the model could 'fix' the examples a paper is about. It only reduces edits, so it cannot invent content or change voice.
checks.proposed_v15_text: tells.md section 9 (When not to act), first bullet: Also leave a pattern alone when the text is talking about it rather than using it, for example a paper, log or guide that names 'delve' or 'It's not X, it's Y' as an example of an AI tell.

checks.reason: v14 is too broad here. T8 lists "'Let me know if…'" as chatbot residue with the fix 'Delete.' A user's own 'let me know if Thursday works' is the request itself, so deleting it would drop content (hard rule 2) and normal correspondence (hard rule 4). messages.md already allows greetings and sign-offs ('A greeting is optional'; 'sign off plainly'), so narrowing T8 makes the files agree. The refinement does not conflict with examples.md #6, which removes a generic closer as part of rewriting an AI-sounding email, not a request inside the user's own message.
checks.proposed_v15_text: tells.md T8 (Chatbot residue): This entry is about an assistant talking to its user ('I hope this helps', 'Let me know if you'd like me to expand this'). In the user's own message, a greeting, a sign-off or a 'let me know' that asks the reader for something ('let me know by Friday if you can drive') is ordinary correspondence; keep it.

checks.reason: The need is real: the dash rule must not touch '--' in LaTeX ranges or command flags. But it is fully covered by the H26 proposal, which keeps code, commands, paths, URLs, LaTeX markup and citation keys exactly as they are, 'dashes and hyphens included'. A separate rule would repeat it.

This conflicts with v14 and does nothing for the prose. SKILL.md step 5 says: "Never wrap the text in 'Here's your revised version!' or end with offers." tells.md T8 lists "Let me know if…" as chatbot residue to delete, and catalog P1 includes "Would you like me to...". The Detect output example (examples.md #10) ends on its last finding. For an application essay, an offer to edit would also break Coach ("You do not write the essay, rephrase their sentences").

v14 already covers this, and the rule has no effect on the prose. Step 1 says "If the material is thin, ask for it before drafting", and Write says "ask two or three targeted questions first." A model asked to improve a draft it was never given asks for it without any rule, and our test record has no case where this failed. It would only lengthen SKILL.md. DEVLOG 24 showed that even moving the mode table within SKILL.md changed the school-essay results, so SKILL.md edits are not free.

(a) no-ai-slop needs this rule to hold back its own "Lead with the point when the setup adds nothing." v14 has no front-loading rule at the paragraph level. Step 2's "Start with the first real claim, scene or result" applies only to the opening, and the genre notes ask for other shapes: explanations "start from a question a reader actually has... show the reasoning step by step", and appeals "Start where the writer's reason starts... Put the ask at the end". (b) The evidence is misread. The tidy structure our judges cited was never a point-first template. In DEVLOG 21 it was bookends, returning motifs and paragraphs that explain their scene at the end (PE11 and personal-essay.md's "Comment once" cover this, and they cut tidy-structure ratings from 86% to 51%). In DEVLOG 22 it was an assembled plan with every part in order (messages.md: "Do not build every appeal from the same parts in the same order"). In DEVLOG 23 it was problem-solution arcs and "First... Second..." (research.md "Stitch and balance"). Each is already handled where it was measured. (c) Sameness of paragraph size and shape is covered by the "Even rhythm" item in SKILL.md, tells R2 ("let length follow content"), S6 and C4. (d) Edit keeps "their sentences and their order... paragraphing", so the rule could not apply there. (e) School argument essays are taught with topic sentences. An unmeasured generic structure rule is the kind of diagnosis-driven rule that did not transfer in DEVLOG 15 (v6).

Partly covered already: T3 has truly, honestly and genuinely; step 4 and personal-essay.md treat actually, really and basically as speech filler; tells section 6 has crucial and "rather than simply"; and sentence-initial Importantly falls under the Additionally/Notably cluster rule. The eight new words are unmeasured. "Just", "simply" and "actually" are ordinary human words, and tells section 10 keeps "casual qualifiers in informal writing" as a human signal. Adding word lists goes against the catalog's evidence that bans backfire (section 1.5, O6, Antislop) and against Edit's "Keep everything else: ... vocabulary". The keep-clause is broad enough that the rule adds no guidance. EB3 (clean learner-essay half, not causal): no-ai-slop, which carries this list, changed 52% of words and 5.1 statements per essay (4% judged the writer's own), against v14's 23%, 2.3 and 60%.

The useful part is already in v14: "it's important to note", "it's worth noting" and "in today's fast-paced world" (tells section 6), self-signposting such as "In this essay I will explore" (S3; catalog P2 lists "Let's dive in"), and the blog-post note. The rest would cut things human writers do. Catalog section 12 lists "in order to" as a human construction. Admitted essays contain clichés of the "at the end of the day" kind (personal-essay.md section 1: "several contain a cliché"; short-answers.md: "sometimes a cliché or a stock transition"). "In terms of" and "with regard to" are ordinary academic register, which research.md keeps. "At its core" is graded as declining (catalog P3). Nothing in our test record measures any of these phrases.

No source in the catalog or the DEVLOG treats capitalization after a colon as an AI sign. Style guides differ (APA capitalizes a full sentence after a colon, Chicago does not), so in Edit the rule would change a writer's correct style, against "Keep everything else: ... punctuation habits". The colon-reveal problem behind it is already handled by tells R5 and the Format row ("a colon only before a list, quote or link").

Almost all of it is already in v14. tells section 7 and the Format row cover bullets where an argument belongs, emoji in formal text (messages.md: emoji only in chat, and only if the user uses them), Title Case and "a heading every 100 words... headings only where a reader navigates" (which includes headers over tiny sections), bold run-in labels and Markdown residue. Only emphasis bold is missing. Catalog F3 grades it C/A only and quotes Anthropic saying earlier models overused bold; Graphite's format measures are declining. Nothing in our test record shows current Claude bolding words in essays, abstracts, appeals or emails. In Edit, removing a writer's own bold would break the minimum-edit rule. Low value and unmeasured, so the default is false.

v14 already has the avoidance half: R6 says "Default: avoid them", a user's own drafts or style rules override it, and messages.md says to leave the user's punctuation. The new half allows 1-2 dashes in long drafts Claude writes, and it does not hold up. (a) The DEVLOG 21/24 dash gap comes from a surface classifier, not from what readers noticed. None of the 16 judge cues coded in DEVLOG 21 is dashes. Adding a mark because it separates real from model text is editing to a detector (tells section 8; section 10, "never fake them"). (b) The feature counts em dashes, en dashes, " - " and "--" (scripts/style_features.py, features.py) in web-published copies. DEVLOG 21 already found publishing artifacts in those copies (curly quotes, double spaces). So the data do not show students choosing em dashes. (c) The genre where the gap was measured, application essays, is Coach mode, which the skill never writes. (d) The readers this user faces treat dashes as an AI sign (R6), and the project's research-paper skill bans them outright. It is worth a reader test, not a rule.

This does nothing in practice. Rebuild ("First check each of its facts"), Detect ("Quote the passages") and Edit ("keep... their order") all assume the model has read the whole text. Our record has no case of an edit made before reading the draft, and the rule has no effect on the output.

(1) It is mostly covered. Hard rule 2 already states what the check would test: "every claim, hedge and number survives unless the user agrees to cut it. Never make a claim stronger than its evidence." Step 4 is not limited to one mode, and its fact diff lists "every name, number, date, quote and claim in the output". Step 5 names "a number flag" among Edit's outputs, and the v14 probe (DEVLOG 25) shows Edit flagging a wrong percentage. (2) The one version of this idea we have tested did not keep meaning. no-ai-slop's own eval.md self-check, whose item 1 is the meaning check, sat in a skill that changed 5.08 statements per learner essay and 3.09 per abstract, with 0-2% of edits clean, against v14's 2.29 and 0.33 (EB3_results.json; the abstract half is affected by the trigger-message problem in the EB3 README). (3) Part of v14's remaining change rate (DEVLOG 25: 0.50 per abstract, 1.06 per learner essay) comes from changes v14 asks for: research.md says "remove only the problems listed below (inflation, hedges they did not mean...)", and Edit says "Cut clear AI tells". A "same strength in every sentence" check would contradict those rules. One gap is real: Edit never says which of step 4's checks it runs (fact diff and numbers, yes; the kicker and rhythm rewrites, no). That needs a one-line scoping fix, tested with the S15 condition in EB3, not this rule.

Step 4 already re-checks after fixes: "Did the rewrite create new tells? ... Count them... rewrite the others." An open fix-and-recheck loop on a person's own text adds passes, and each pass is another chance to edit more. That is the over-editing tells section 8 warns about and DEVLOG 24 measured (plain "improve" changed 75-90% of words). no-ai-slop, which requires this loop, changed 52% of learner-essay words against v14's 23% (EB3). The loop also runs eval.md checks that v14 contradicts, such as active voice and banned words.

v14 removed this on purpose. v13.1 step 5 said "add at most three lines on what changed and why". The v14 audit found that this contradicted the mode outputs, and v14 settled on one format: the text, then only what the mode calls for (DEVLOG 25 point 1; changelog: "One output format for Edit and Coach"). Bringing it back reopens the contradiction. The changes a writer needs in order to check meaning are already reported: hard rule 2 ("If you cut a sentence because it is a tell... say so after the text"), the number flag, Rebuild's one line and Coach's list of fixes. Listing every routine error fix is noise, breaks step 5's "in a few lines", and does not change the prose.

The nearest v14 genre is explanations, and v14's tested advice there points the other way: "A sequence of textbook definitions is what reads as machine-made" (SKILL.md, Genre notes). A general line saying neutral reference prose is fine would license the flat, polished register our judges read as AI. "Flat, plain register" was cited as AI in 28 to 42% of ratings of model essays (DEVLOG 21). "Fluent, polished, frictionless prose" was cited in 83 to 96% of ratings of model abstracts (DEVLOG 23). A user's own encyclopedic draft is already protected by Edit ("Keep everything else: their sentences and their order, vocabulary..."). tells.md 9 also guards it ("Genre conventions"; "A non-native writer's formal style. Do not push it toward a template"). No test case exists, and our users rarely write this genre.

Already covered in several places. Hard rule 4: "leave strong sentences alone, including the writer's odd word choices, asides and mixed feelings." Edit: "Keep everything else: their sentences and their order, vocabulary, repetitions, paragraphing, contractions, humor and punctuation habits." tells.md preamble: unmarked entries such as S9 act only on a pattern, "not on one instance." S12: "Fine once if it is the writer's real habit of speech." tells.md 10 keeps "parenthetical asides" and "endings that stop on a specific point". personal-essay.md keeps "a side detail the student cared about", which is the digressions cue from DEVLOG 21, already imported. short-answers rule 8: "a fragment or a list is fine." No failure has been observed: v14's Edit text, run as v13.1, stayed within a few points of an errors-only copyedit and kept voice at 9 to 10 (DEVLOG 24). Adding the rule would also do harm. A line praising fragments and abrupt endings leaks into Write mode, and v7's "honest open question" rule produced shrugging endings (DEVLOG 21). tells.md 8 already lists fragment runs as an over-correction.

The core idea is already covered. Edit says "If the user also gave a writing sample, it overrides the default style rules here." The mode section says "When a project has its own writing rules ... follow them too; they win on conflicts." In Claude Code, CLAUDE.md and project skills already serve as the standing file (GreenBERT uses research-paper). The addition would also do harm. Auto-reading a fixed filename from any working directory turns repository content into instructions, which is an injection surface. Its "banned phrases" part is the word-list approach our record rates weak (DEVLOG 1.1: word lists lift 0.9; the SKILL.md Words pass says "do not just swap the word"). A stored voice sample also makes it easier to produce text in a student's voice, which Coach forbids for application essays. It is untested.

Marketing is not a v14 genre, and a fixed template would create a known tell. Short paragraphs, then benefits, then a call to action is the "assembled plan" judges caught in appeals: a tidy plan was cited in 50 to 59% of model judgments against 12% of real ones (DEVLOG 22). messages.md rule 3 already says "Do not build every appeal from the same parts in the same order." Uniformly short paragraphs conflict with tells.md R2 ("let length follow content"). Where the ask goes is already in messages.md rule 2. Concrete benefits can only come from the user's facts (rule 4, hard rule 1).

C6 covers unsourced proof ("name the source and what it said, or cut the claim. Never invent a source"), and T1 and S8 cover inflation and triads. The proposed fix, one source and what it said, needs a fact users rarely supply, so under hard rule 1 it reduces to [ask:] or a cut. On the user's own text, cutting a real list of press coverage removes claims, which breaks hard rule 2 ("every claim ... survives unless the user agrees to cut it"). Lists of real honors are normal in our genres (short-answers.md: "Honors: the name of the award and its level"), and judges cited "résumé lists" as a sign of a real student (DEVLOG 21). No case in our record.

The substance is covered. C1: "A sentence that could move unchanged into another person's essay or another company's report says nothing." C2 covers categories used in place of instances. A line like "from small startups to global corporations" fails both tests. The literal fix, naming the actual items, needs items the user may not have given (hard rule 1). Real ranges ("from 140 TL to 500 TL") are ordinary human writing. This is a phrase-level rule, the kind our evidence ranks lowest (SKILL.md: "fix content first and vocabulary last"). It is not in our catalog and was never observed in tests.

T8 already says to delete chatbot residue ("Great question", "I hope this helps", "Certainly!"), and cutoff disclaimers belong to the same class. The fact the disclaimer hedged is handled by the step 4 fact diff ("Remove or bracket anything that does not" come from the user or source). Rebuild also says to "restore hedges and admissions the draft dropped". The humanizer's literal fix is unsafe: "state the fact" without the fact breaks hard rule 1, and cutting a real hedge breaks hard rule 2. Catalog P9 notes these hedges are mainly a GPT-6 habit ("Claude drafts are less prone").

This would remove something human writers do. Catalog section 12 lists "Isolated wordy constructions humans use ('in order to', 'the fact that')" as a human signal. tells.md 9 says one weak tell alone never justifies an edit, and hard rule 4 requires the minimum edit on human text. For text Claude writes, "Use plain verbs" and the plain-verb swaps in tells.md 6 already cover the useful part.

This conflicts with the explanations note ("start from a question a reader actually has"). Question headings are normal in FAQs, explainers and blog posts, and blog posts are where v14 already strips too much (DEVLOG 15: "The skill's audit may strip the looseness these genres want"). The heading problems we have evidence for are already in tells.md 7 (Title Case, "a heading every 100 words"). Nothing in our record shows question headings reading as AI.

The "fill in" half is already covered and limited by hard rule 1 ("ask, or write [ask: ...]") and by messages.md's check for "a sign-off name you made up". A stray placeholder in the user's text blocks the meaning, and Edit already fixes "anything that blocks the meaning". The "delete" half is harmful: v14's own output contains [ask: ...] and [cite: ...] brackets that a user may paste back for another pass. Some placeholders are also deliberate (a mail merge, a team message template with [name]).

Covered in kind by tells.md 7 ("Markdown residue (`**`, `##`) in text pasted into Word or a form. Remove.") and by Edit ("anything that blocks the meaning"). The source pointer the token carried is handled by research.md ("If a claim needs a source, write [cite: source for X]") and the fact diff. Naming bracketed "[cite: N]" forms as markup to delete causes concrete harm: it collides with v14's own [cite: source for X] placeholders. A second pass on a skill-edited paper would strip them and leave claims unsourced, which research.md forbids ("'Studies show' with no citation is not acceptable"). These tokens come from other chatbots, not Claude, and never appeared in our tests. Scrubbing the most visible marker of pasted chatbot text also leans toward concealment, which the Integrity section rules out ("It is not a way to hide AI use").

Spelling errors are already fixed under Edit ("Fix outright errors (spelling, grammar...)"). Mixed US/UK spelling is common in non-native human writers, and v14 says "do not make the phrasing sound native". The register part, "rewrite AI sections to match the author", requires deciding which sections are AI, which v14 forbids. Detect: "Do not guess whether a human or a model wrote it." Rebuild applies only when the user says an AI wrote the text: "if you only suspect it, use Edit, since tells are not proof of authorship." For application essays and graded work, it would make AI text pass as the student's own (hard rule 5, Integrity). Mixed registers are an ineffective indicator (catalog 13), and real essays mixed plain and "reaching vocabulary" (DEVLOG 21).

Same as P02. C6, T1 and S8 cover it. The fix needs what the outlet reported, which only the user can supply (hard rule 1), so it reduces to [ask:] or a cut. Cutting a real list of coverage on the user's own text removes claims without their agreement (hard rule 2). The humanizer's own example invents the profile it cites.

v14 covers the form our evidence supports: tells.md 7 bold run-in labels and Markdown residue. Evidence for scattered bold is weak and declining (catalog F3, Graphite "declining"). The one sighting in our record counted as warmth, not as a tell (LEDGER case 1: "Plain sample 2 came next (polite address to teachers, a heart emoji, the amount in bold)"), and chat users bold amounts themselves. Stripping bold from the user's own text breaks the minimum edit (hard rule 4). The "glossary terms and UI labels" exception is a rule for technical documentation, which the skill does not serve.

Covered by tells.md R3 ("give sentences real subjects (people, the school, the writer)") and by T4 for personifying metaphors. In research, "Table 2 shows" is a convention (research.md) and "the data show" is standard. Naming an actor the source does not name breaks hard rule 1. The "use you" fix was tested and dropped: "v5's 'talk to the reader as you' rule dropped (no measurable effect)" (DEVLOG 13).

It gives the reader nothing and can damage text. These characters are invisible or look identical, so removing them changes only what machines see, while v14 exists for good writing for "its reader" (hard rule 3, Integrity). Non-breaking spaces and soft hyphens are legitimate typography (between a number and its unit; French and Turkish typesetting). Mapping look-alike letters can corrupt real Greek, Cyrillic or Turkish text (DEVLOG 21: a Greek-letter artifact misled judges). The user's request frames this as watermark removal. Claude's watermark mechanism is not public and "may persist through some editing" (DEVLOG 1.5), so this cannot honestly be offered as watermark removal, and offering it that way conflicts with the Integrity section ("It is not a way to hide AI use"). Stripping look-alike letters inserted by a bypass tool also erases the evidence of an attempt to evade detection.

Covered by R1 ("Vary length where the meaning changes pace ... Never chop at random"). A hard rule against three similar sentences forces chopping that research.md rule 3 forbids ("do not chop it into short sentences"). tells.md 8 lists that chopping as an over-correction ("Chopping sentences into fragments for 'burstiness'"). Real abstracts average 23 words per sentence (DEVLOG 23). "Short punchy beats" were cited as AI in 42 to 57% of ratings of plain and word-list essays (DEVLOG 21).

Optimizing an opening for effect is exactly what judges caught: labeled-object and campus-trivia hooks (short-answers.md rule 3, DEVLOG 23) and the engineered essay (PE11). v14's tested guidance favors plain openings. short-answers.md: "a plain statement of the answer ... is fine and common." personal-essay.md: admitted essays "open in many ways ... a plain fact" and "differ from one another far more than model versions do". Research starts from the problem; action messages put the news first. A tournament the model judges itself would pick the most crafted hook and make openings more alike. DEVLOG 12 records a similar case: v5's example stance line became the opening in 3 of 4 arguments. It is also barred in Edit (hard rule 4) and Coach (hard rule 5).

"3-5 sentence paragraphs" conflicts with tells.md R2 ("Every paragraph four sentences. Fix: let length follow content"). "Dry wit" is the comic aside judges flagged (short-answers.md rule 3, DEVLOG 23). A preset applied across genres is the "One register for everything" tell in SKILL.md, while v14 sets register by genre and by the writer's own sample. Examples would have to come from the user anyway (hard rule 1).

"Encouragement" and "acknowledge difficulty" are the additions our record caught plain Claude inventing in a group message: a feeling and an apology the sender never stated (LEDGER case 1, messages.md rule 9). messages.md rule 3 says to leave out parts "the writer would not bother with". Uniformly short paragraphs conflict with R2. Warmth, contractions and forms of address are already set by genre and by the user (messages.md rules 6 and 7). Untested.

As worded, it would do harm. Declaring fiction out of scope would remove hard rules 1 and 5 from a graded creative-writing assignment or a creative college supplement, and v14 must still coach those (Coach covers "schoolwork the user says will be graded or handed in as their own"). The narrower point, that fiction has its own conventions (dialogue beats, fragments, one-line paragraphs), has no test evidence in our record. v14's pattern-level guards already limit damage to a story (tells.md preamble; S9 and S11 act only on repeated patterns). Fiction would need its own benchmark first, as every v14 genre had.

The evidence does not show a language effect. v8's failure on Turkish (DEVLOG 22) came from the general Format rule pushing semicolons and colons, from the opening rule and from spoken tics carried over from the notes. The v9 fix was mostly language-general (no semicolons, a written rather than spoken voice, one part carrying the text). The one Turkish-specific item, the circumflex, already sits in messages.md. Structural tells do cross languages: our catalog cites Peng et al. measuring corrective framing in Mandarin (DEVLOG 19). An 'English-only' note could lead the model to drop the hard rules or the minimum edit for other languages, and v14 bundles no detector for the note to scope.

Already covered. Hard rule 4 says 'Fix what is broken; leave strong sentences alone' and Edit says 'Keep everything else'. Editing only the section the user names is ordinary instruction-following. There is no evidence either way, and the line would add words to a SKILL.md that loads on every use.

Already covered. Hard rule 2 keeps instruction-like lines ('every claim, hedge and number survives unless the user agrees to cut it'), and so does Edit ('Keep everything else: their sentences and their order'). Not obeying text inside a draft is base model behaviour against prompt injection, not a writing rule. The comparer agrees it has little effect on prose.

Covered where it matters. tells.md sec 9 says 'When not to act: Quotations, titles, names, and text written before late 2022', which includes quoted ESG claims and quoted tell specimens in the papers. SKILL.md says 'Skip it for code, data tables', and research.md keeps 'the way they name their own variables and groups'. URLs, paths and frontmatter are not prose the skill edits. Reporting findings inside quotations would lengthen the output against step 5 ('in a few lines').

It conflicts with v14's measured default. For a user's own text v14 uses Edit, a minimum edit even when the user says 'improve it'. 'Rewrite by default' is the behaviour DEVLOG 24 measured as harmful: 75 to 90 percent of words changed, 3 to 4 statements added, and 0 to 27 percent judged the writer's own. The detect mapping already exists ('Detect / review (user asks "does this sound like AI?"...'). In-place file editing is tooling.

The cited evidence is misread. DEVLOG 1.1 says blader's rewrites made rhythm more uniform and added aphoristic closers; it does not attribute this to the number of passes. A cap would also collide with v14's procedure. Personal essays use two drafting passes by design (step 2), and step 4 can trigger a further corrective rewrite (the kicker count). Reporting pass counts conflicts with step 5 ('in a few lines'). Nothing in our data ties quality to pass count.

The legitimate part is covered: Edit already keeps the writer's 'punctuation habits'. tells.md sec 9 lists 'curly quotes' as a weak tell that never justifies an edit alone. The only evidence offered (DEVLOG 21) is that quote style showed which texts a model wrote, and that came from separate texts, not quote styles mixed inside one edited document. A step whose stated payoff is removing that provenance cue sits against the Integrity section ('It is not a way to hide AI use'), especially in a run prompted by a watermark-remover request. It is untested and depends on a node script v14 does not ship.

v14 already ranks by evidence. It says 'fix content first and vocabulary last', marks tells strong or weak (tells.md intro) and audits in content-first order. Their P0 tier puts surface artifacts at the top. That runs against catalog sec 1 item 4 (experts catch AI by content and structure) and DEVLOG 21 (tidy structure was the dominant cue, 75 to 86 percent).

Covered by v14's precedence rule: 'When a project has its own writing rules ... follow them too; they win on conflicts', which reads naturally onto a guide the user names. A status line adds output that step 5 keeps short. There is no evidence for it.
Formatting only, with no evidence. Edit keeps the writer's 'paragraphing', and tells.md sec 7 already handles markup residue in pasted text. It does nothing for the prose.

Not covered. Step 4's fact diff only confirms that names, numbers and claims in the output come from the source, so a reworded sentence that shifts meaning still passes, and nothing enforces hard rule 4 after the fact. The residue is measured: DEVLOG 25 has v13.1 'improve' edits changing 0.50 statements per abstract and 1.06 per learner essay, with 31 percent of learner essays unchanged in meaning against 56 percent for the errors-only copyedit. DEVLOG 24's ablation found that the explicit checks in SKILL.md carry the fidelity behaviour, so a matching check for edits is the natural lever. It adds no content and no visible tell. It is untested, and the held-out edit halves are already worn (DEVLOG 25), so it needs a fresh set before any gain is claimed.
checks.proposed_v15_text: SKILL.md, step 4 (Check before returning), a new bullet after the fact diff, for Edit and for Coach corrections: Put your version next to the writer's and look at each place they differ. Every difference must fix an outright error, clear up something that blocks the meaning, remove a clear AI tell or meet something the user asked for (such as a word limit); anything else goes back to the writer's own words, and the notes after the text mention only changes that are actually in it.

checks.reason: This is general instruction-following, not a writing rule. v14 has no transformation-request type, our data has no evidence on it, and it would add words to SKILL.md.

It conflicts with step 5: 'in a few lines unless they asked for a full critique'. DEVLOG 16 already found Coach feedback too long for a student (2,264 words). v14 runs no tools or checks that could fail to run, so 'name checks that did not run' has nothing to attach to.
Covered. v14 Detect says 'Lead with the most important problem' and examples.md #10 sets the format. Severity tiers and a detector line are formatting, and v14 bundles no detector.

Coach already lists each fix where a student learns from the list (personal-essay.md sec 8: 'first each fix, quoting the original words'). For an 'improve it' request, a per-edit before/after list for a learner essay with many fixes breaks step 5's brevity. v14 has no validator.

Already adopted. SKILL.md Credits say the "'Never inject' guardrails" were adapted from this same repo. Hard rule 1 bans any fact, feeling or anecdote the user did not supply, and that also governs C3. 'Now more than ever' fails the C1 portability test, and tells.md sec 6 already lists 'in today's fast-paced world'.

tells.md sec 7 already removes bold run-in labels and Markdown residue ('Remove'). v14's genres (essays, abstracts, emails, appeals) rarely carry bold. In a user's own document the bold is theirs (hard rule 4). The only evidence is grade C/A.
No evidence in our catalog. 'Worth a look' with no reason is covered by T2 (a rating instead of a description) and C1 (portability).

It contradicts v14's 'Rewrite the sentence around its claim; do not just swap the word'. Word lists show little value in our data: held-out word list vs plain +1.9 [-2.2, +6.0] (DEVLOG 21), and removing tells.md did not lower human-likeness (DEVLOG 24 ablation). Catalog sec 1 item 5 (Antislop) warns of a backfire, and the tier's frequency claim is admitted to be unmeasured.

A 3 percent trigger almost never fires and would undercut research.md's 'Inflate the result. novel, innovative, promising, significant (without a test)', which rests on measured evidence (catalog RP2).
Crypto and marketing boilerplate is outside the skill's genres. The source's replacement advice ('Describe the actual mechanism') invites invented content, against hard rule 1.

It would drop a measured Claude-era tell. v14 example 7 targets exactly the predicative use ('This assumption is quietly load-bearing'), and Abraham's 39x measure (catalog V9) counts the word in any position. tells.md sec 9 already exempts the engineering sense.

T3 covers the class ('Intensifiers and sincerity markers. genuinely, truly ... Fix: delete'). 'Real' and 'true' are ordinary words in student writing, tells.md sec 10 keeps casual qualifiers, and hard rule 4 protects them in a writer's own text. No specific evidence.
Covered by T4 (mannered prose, 'Fix: the literal statement') and T3 ('honestly'). The only evidence comes from GitHub pull-request text, graded C/U for essays (catalog V9).

In Write, hard rule 1 already bars a scope claim the user did not supply. Rebuild treats 'A generalization stated as fact' as an error. In Edit, dropping 'every' changes the writer's claim, which hard rule 2 forbids without agreement.
No evidence in our catalog or data. 'Turns into' and 'becomes' are ordinary narration in essays, and the mannered cases are already covered by T4 ('say the literal thing').
The source admits its six-tag threshold is not validated. Trimming a user's own tags breaks hard rule 4, and our data has nothing on hashtags.
tells.md sec 7 covers bullets where an argument belongs. Verbless feature lists are rare in the skill's genres, and no evidence was offered.
No evidence. research.md treats agentless or passive procedure as a convention ('Passive voice is normal for procedures'), and hard rule 1 already bars naming an actor the source does not give.
Covered by C1 (generic examples any writer could use), S8 (forced triads) and Rebuild ('its examples, analogies and paragraph plan are the stock answer'). The only evidence is grade C.

Covered by S3 run-ups ('Fix: start with the claim'), research.md 'Open on the world, not the problem' and the explanations note ('start from a question a reader actually has'). A blanket cut would also hit appeals, where messages.md allows openers like 'Did you know...?' because real pre-2022 appeals use them.
No evidence in our catalog. Covered by C2 (categories instead of instances) and C1. The source condition it needs is hard rule 1 anyway.

Not an AI tell. Edit already fixes outright errors, and spellings like 'data-set' are variants, not errors, so changing them breaks hard rule 4. DEVLOG 21 found wrong hyphens among real students' human traces.
Covered by the class rule in T8, chatbot residue ('Delete').
In Write and Rebuild, hard rule 1 and the fact diff already catch unsupported guesses. In the user's own text 'is believed to have' is a hedge that hard rule 2 keeps.
Hard rule 1 already bars filling a placeholder with invented content, and v14's own `[ask: ...]` and `[cite: ...]` brackets show it leaves gaps visible rather than guessing.

The prose half is covered: tells.md sec 7 removes residue pasted from a tool ('Remove'), research.md marks a missing source as `[cite: source for X]`, and hard rule 1 bars inventing a citation. The source repo calls these tokens 'fingerprints' that prove which chat tool wrote the text, so a named rule to strip them is provenance removal. The Integrity section rules that out, and this run was prompted by a watermark-remover request.
It does nothing for the prose. Its only AI-specific effect is removing a provenance marker, which conflicts with Integrity: 'It is not a way to hide AI use.'
Covered. research.md lists 'Inflate the result. novel, innovative...' (RP4), S2 and S3 cover staging such as 'what nobody tells you', hard rule 1 applies in Write and hard rule 2 in Edit.
Covered by T4 (metaphor performing cleverness, 'Fix: the literal statement') and research.md ('One concept, one name'; domain terms each defined once). No evidence in our catalog.
Product launch copy is outside the genres the skill was built and tested on.
These social-post closers are outside the skill's genres. Covered by S7 (upbeat send-offs) and T8.

Its safeguard is already a hard rule: 'Never make a claim stronger than its evidence ... never put a position the writer did not take in its place' (hard rule 2). T6's fix is bounded by 'the position the evidence supports and say how strong it is', and the doubt cases are in short-answers rule 4 and personal-essay sec 5 ('keep it at the strength they hold it'). DEVLOG 23's failure came from s1's 'whole-heartedly' rule, which v10.1 fixed; it did not come from T6.

S3 already catches staged questions ('The answer? Simple.'). Rhetorical questions are normal in student argument essays, and messages.md allows openers like 'Did you know...?' for appeals on evidence from real pre-2022 appeals. No evidence for a general cut.

It conflicts with measured evidence and with v14. Parentheses are a human signal (catalog F2: LLMs use 'hardly any parentheses'), and tells.md sec 10 keeps 'parenthetical asides'. Hard rule 4 protects a writer's asides.
Covered by research.md (counted framing 'that the notes do not count'), S8 (forced triads) and S3 (signposts).
S3 already lists 'Let's break this down', and T8 covers chatbot residue. tells.md sec 9 exempts numbered steps.
No evidence in our appeal or message data. Edit keeps the writer's 'paragraphing'.

Covered by messages.md (the news and the request in the first two lines), T8 and T9. A blanket cut would also hurt cold emails to professors, where naming the recipient's specific work is a convention, not flattery.
Covered by tells.md sec 7 ('headings only where a reader navigates'). It would need the sec 9 exemption for papers anyway.
Software marketing slogans are outside the skill's genres.
Covered by S11 (at most one or two kicker endings), S9 (fragment stacks) and R5 (no semicolons added).

The trigger points the wrong way. tells.md R4 says 'AI text is more lexically varied than human text', and the catalog's measurements (Graphite, Creanga & Dinu) agree, so a low TTR is more likely human.

Adding bridges is what our data says to avoid. Connective observations were the engineered-essay cue in DEVLOG 21, and removing them in v8b raised p(real) by +6.3 and cut unsupported claims from 1.50 to 0.12 per essay. research.md lists 'Stitch and balance' as a model sign. The reporting half is already in personal-essay sec 5 ('Each paragraph should move the story or the thinking forward').

It conflicts with the evidence behind the classic list (Kobak's excess vocabulary in scientific abstracts, catalog RP1/V1). 'Test harness' and 'ecosystem' are not on v14's lists, so there is nothing to exempt.
This is internal logic for a voice-profile system that v14 does not have.
Covered by messages.md rule 7 ('Address readers the way the writer would') and T8.

v14 already lets a sample override the defaults ('it overrides the default style rules here, including the dash rule'). It also warns against numeric targets: 'These describe the genre; they are not targets. Do not add long sentences or lessons to hit a number' (personal-essay.md sec 1). Our record shows the risk: the v8 candidate's register targets produced a flat, stiff register (42 percent flat, 11 percent stiff) and its round 1 gain did not replicate (-0.2, DEVLOG 21). Matching 'recurring words' and 'paragraph openings' invites caricature and R3's repeated openers. It is untested.
